**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 1 of 10):**

[On] the basmalah (the formula "In the name of God") and it contains twenty-seven issues.

[Surah al-Fatihah (1): verse 1]

﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾ (1)

His saying, exalted is He: The first issue. The scholars said: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" is an oath from our Lord, which He sent down at the beginning of every surah. He swears to His servants that what He has set forth for you, O My servants, in this surah is true, and that I will fulfill for you everything I have included in this surah of My promise, My kindness, and My goodness. "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" is among what God, exalted is He, sent down in His Book, and especially upon this community, after Solomon, peace be upon him. Some scholars said: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" comprises the whole of the Law (shari'ah), because it indicates the Essence and the Attributes, and this is correct.

The second issue: Sa'id ibn Abi Sukayna said: It has reached me that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, looked at a man writing "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" and said to him: "Make it beautiful, for a man who made it beautiful was forgiven." Sa'id said: It has also reached me that a man looked at a sheet on which "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" was written, so he kissed it and placed it on his eyes, and he was forgiven. From this meaning is the story of Bishr al-Hafi, for when he picked up the scrap on which was the name of God, and perfumed it, his name was perfumed. [[The text of the story as in Wafayat al-A'yan and al-Risalah al-Qushayriyyah: "... The cause of his repentance was that he found on the road a paper on which the name of God, mighty and majestic, was written, and it had been trodden upon by feet. He took it and, with some dirhams he had, bought perfume and scented the paper with it, and placed it in a crack in a wall. He saw in a dream as if someone was saying to him: 'O Bishr, you perfumed My name, so I will perfume you in this world and the next.' When he woke from his sleep, he repented."]] Al-Qushayri mentioned it. Al-Nasa'i related from Abu al-Malih, from Ridf of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When your mount stumbles, do not say, 'May Satan perish,' for he swells until he becomes like a house and says, 'By my power I did it.' Rather say, 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful,' for he shrinks until he becomes like a fly." 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, in his interpretation of His saying: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn their backs in aversion﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 271.]], said: Its meaning is: when you say "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." Waki' related from al-A'mash, from Abu Wa'il, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: Whoever wishes that God save him from the nineteen guardians of Hell, let him recite "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," so that God makes for him, for each letter of it, a shield from each one of them. Thus the basmalah has nineteen letters, corresponding to the number of the angels of the Fire, concerning whom God said: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [74:30]; and they say in all their actions, "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." Hence it is their strength, and by the name of God they are made strong. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: A parallel to this is their saying about the Night of Power that it is the night of the twenty-seventh, out of regard for the word "hiya" (it) among the words of the surah "Indeed We sent it down" [97]. A parallel to this also is their saying about the number of the angels who hastened to write the words of the one who says: "Our Lord, and to You be praise, abundant, good, blessed in it," for it is some thirty-odd letters. Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw some thirty angels hastening to write it, each wanting to be first to write it." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is among the witty remarks of tafsir and not among the solid knowledge.

The third issue: al-Sha'bi and al-A'mash related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to write "In Your name, O God" until he was commanded to write "In the name of God," and he wrote it. Then when the verse was revealed: ﴿Say: Call upon God or call upon the Most Gracious﴾ [17:110], he wrote "In the name of God, the Most Gracious." Then when the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ [27:30], he wrote it. In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, al-Sha'bi, Abu Malik, Qatadah and Thabit ibn 'Umarah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) did not write "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" until the surah "al-Naml" was revealed.

The fourth issue: It is related from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him, that he said: The basmalah is the crowns of the surahs. I say: This indicates that it is not a verse of al-Fatihah nor of any other surah. The scholars differed on this. (The first view) it is not a verse of al-Fatihah nor of any other, and this is the view of Malik. (The second) it is a verse of every surah, and this is the view of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak. (The third) al-Shafi'i said: It is a verse in al-Fatihah, and his view wavered regarding the rest of the surahs: at one time he said it is a verse of every surah, and at another he said it is not a verse except in al-Fatihah alone. There is no disagreement among them that it is a verse of the Qur'an in surah al-Naml. Al-Shafi'i argued with what al-Daraqutni related from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Hanafi, from 'Abd al-Hamid [[This hadith is found in the sources in a confused form; the correction is from Sunan al-Daraqutni and Tahdhib al-Tahdhib. This 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far is called Abu al-Fadl, and it is said: Abu Hafs, and Abu Bakr is not his kunyah. Abu Bakr al-Hanafi related from him. See Tahdhib al-Tahdhib.]] ibn Ja'far, from Nuh ibn Abi Bilal, from Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id al-Maqburi, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When you recite ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, then recite ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, for it is the Mother of the Qur'an, the Mother of the Book, and the seven oft-repeated, and ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is one of its verses." 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far raised this hadith. And this 'Abd al-Hamid was declared reliable by Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Yahya ibn Sa'id, and Yahya ibn Ma'in; and Abu Hatim said of him: "His station is truthfulness," but Sufyan al-Thawri used to discredit him and speak against him. Nuh ibn Abi Bilal is a reliable and well-known transmitter. The proof of Ibn al-Mubarak is the one related by the compilers of the Six (Books)... As for the proof of al-Shafi'i, it is what Muslim related from Anas, who said: One day while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was among us, he dozed off briefly, then raised his head smiling. We said: "What made you laugh, O Messenger of God?" He said: "A surah was just revealed to me," and he recited: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Indeed We have given you al-Kawthar. So pray to your Lord and sacrifice. Indeed, your enemy is the one cut off.﴾" And he related the hadith, and it will come in full in the surah al-Kawthar, God willing [[See vol. 20, p. 216.]].

The fifth issue: The correct view among these opinions is the view of Malik, because the Qur'an is not established by solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad), and its path is definite, mass transmission (tawatur qat'i) which is not disputed. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "It is enough for you that it is not from the Qur'an, the disagreement of people about it, and the Qur'an is not disputed." The sound reports free of any flaw indicate that the basmalah is not a verse of al-Fatihah nor of any other surah, except in al-Naml alone. Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "God, mighty and majestic, said: 'I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves, and My servant shall have what he asks.' When the servant says: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, God says: 'My servant has praised Me.' When he says: ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, God says: 'My servant has extolled Me.' When he says: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, He says: 'My servant has glorified Me'; and once He said: 'He has entrusted (the matter) to My servant.' When he says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, He says: 'This is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks.' When he says: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those You have blessed, not of those who earn anger nor of those who go astray﴾, He says: 'This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks.'"

So His saying, glorified is He: "I have divided the prayer" means al-Fatihah, and He called it "prayer" because the prayer is not valid without it. He made the first three verses for Himself, and they are specific to Him, blessed is His name, and the Muslims did not differ about them. Then He made the fourth verse between Himself and His servant, because it includes the servant's humility and his request for help from Him, and that includes the glorification of God, exalted is He. Then three verses, completing seven verses. Among what indicates that they are three is His saying: "These are for My servant," related by Malik, and He did not say "these two." This indicates that "an'amta 'alayhim" is a verse. Ibn Bukayr said: Malik said: "an'amta 'alayhim" is a verse, then the seventh verse to the end. Thus it is established by this division which God, exalted is He, made, and by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Ubayy: "How do you recite when you begin the prayer?" He said: "I recited, 'Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds,' until I reached its end," that the basmalah is not a verse of it. Likewise the people of Medina, the people of Syria, and the people of Basra counted, and most of the reciters counted "an'amta 'alayhim" as a verse. Likewise Qatadah related from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The sixth verse is "an'amta 'alayhim." As for the Kufan reciters and jurists, they counted "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" in it, and did not count "an'amta 'alayhim."

If it is said: It is established in the Mushaf, written in its (the Companions') script, and transmitted, as it was transmitted in al-Naml, and that is mass-transmitted from them. We say: What you have mentioned is correct, but (it is written) either because it is Qur'an, or because it is a separator between surahs, as was related from the Companions: "We did not know the end of a surah until 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful' was revealed," related by Abu Dawud; or for its blessing, just as the community has agreed upon writing it at the beginnings of books and letters? All of that is possible. Al-Jurayri [[Al-Jurayri (with a damma on the jim, a fatha on the ra, a kasra on the second, and a sukun on the ya between them, a nisba to Jarir ibn 'Abbad ibn Dubay'ah): he is Sa'id ibn Iyas al-Jurayri, Abu Mas'ud al-Basri.]] said: Al-Hasan was asked about "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," and he said: "At the heads of letters." Al-Hasan also said: "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" was not revealed in any part of the Qur'an except in "Ta-Sin," ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾.

The decisive point is that the Qur'an is not established by speculation and inference, but only by definite, compulsory mass transmission. Then the saying of al-Shafi'i has been inconsistent regarding it at the beginning of every surah, which indicates that it is not a verse of every surah, and praise be to God. If it is said: A group has related its being Qur'an, and al-Daraqutni undertook to collect that in a part which he authenticated. We say: We do not deny the narration with that, and we have pointed to it; and we have authentic reports against it, related by the reliable imams and the trustworthy jurists. 'A'ishah related in Sahih Muslim, she said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to begin the prayer with the takbir, and the recitation with "Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds," the hadith... and it will come in full. Muslim also related from Anas ibn Malik, who said: I prayed behind the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and 'Umar, and they used to begin with "Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds," not mentioning "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" either at the beginning of the recitation or at its end. Furthermore, our school is preferred in this by a great consideration, which is the rational one: the Mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ) in Medina has seen ages pass over it and times and eras, from the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) until the time of Malik, and no one ever recited "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" in it, out of following the Sunnah, and this refutes your hadiths. Nevertheless, our companions (the Malikis) regarded reciting it in the supererogatory prayer (nafl) as recommended, and the reports mentioning its recitation at the beginning are to be understood in this light, as a matter of latitude. Malik said: There is no harm in reciting it in the supererogatory prayer, and for one who recites the Qur'an by reading it through (in order).

The school of Malik and his companions holds that it (the basmalah) is not a verse of al-Fatihah or of any other surah. The worshipper does not recite it in the obligatory prayer or in any other prayer, whether silently or aloud, but it is permissible to recite it in voluntary prayers. This is the well-known position of his school. There is another narration from him that it is recited at the beginning of surahs in voluntary prayers, but not at the beginning of Umm al-Qur'an (al-Fatihah). Ibn Nafi' narrated from him that it is recited at the beginning of the recitation in both obligatory and voluntary prayers and must never be omitted under any circumstances.

Among the people of Madinah there are those who say that the basmalah ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ must be recited with al-Fatihah. Among them are Ibn Umar and Ibn Shihab, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr and Abu Ubayd. This indicates that the matter is one of juristic reasoning (ijtihad) and not a definitive (qat'i) matter, contrary to what some ignorant members of the jurists (mutafaqqihah) have supposed, whose view would entail declaring the Muslims disbelievers. It is not as he supposed, because of the existence of the disagreement mentioned, and praise be to God.

A group of scholars has gone to the view of reciting it silently with al-Fatihah, among them Abu Hanifah and al-Thawri. This is narrated from Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ammar and Ibn al-Zubayr, and it is the view of al-Hakam and Hammad. Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Abu Ubayd also said this. The same is narrated from al-Awza'i, as related by Abu Umar ibn Abd al-Barr in (al-Istidhkar).

As for the reports they relied upon in this matter, they cite what Mansur ibn Zadhan narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ prayed with us and did not let us hear the recitation of ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾." And what Ammar ibn Ruzayq [[So in Tahdhib al-Tahdhib; in the originals it reads "Ammar 'an Ruzayq", which is an error.]] narrated from al-A'mash, from Shu'bah, from Thabit, from Anas, who said: "I prayed behind the Prophet ﷺ and behind Abu Bakr and Umar, and I did not hear any of them proclaim ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ aloud."

I say: this is a good opinion, and in agreement with it the reports from Anas are consistent and not contradictory, and by it the disagreement regarding the recitation of the basmalah is resolved.

It is also narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "The polytheists used to attend the mosque, and when the Messenger of God ﷺ recited ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, they would say: 'This is Muhammad mentioning the Rahman of Yamamah,' meaning Musaylimah. So he was commanded to recite ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ in a low voice, and there was revealed: ﴿Do not be loud in your prayer, nor be silent in it﴾."

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu Abd Allah said: "So that remained as this practice (rasm) until our day, even though the reason for it has ceased, just as the ramal in tawaf (quick stepping in the circumambulation) remained even though its reason has ceased, and the silent recitation in daytime prayers remained even though its reason has ceased."

Sixth: The community (ummah) has agreed on the permissibility of writing it at the beginning of every book of knowledge and every treatise. If the book is a diwan of poetry... Mujalid narrated from al-Sha'bi, who said: "They agreed not to write ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ at the head of poetry." Al-Zuhri said: "The sunnah has passed that they do not write ﴿In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ in poetry." Sa'id ibn Jubayr went to writing the basmalah at the beginning of books of poetry, and most later scholars followed him in this. Abu Bakr al-Khatib said: "This is what we choose and prefer."

Seventh: al-Mawardi said: "One who says 'bismillah' is called mubasmil, and this is a later-coined usage (lughah muwalladah), though it has appeared in poetry." Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah said:
"Laylā has said bismillah when I met her, / so how sweet is that beloved one, the one who says bismillah."

I say: the well-known form from the lexicographers is basmala. Ya'qub ibn al-Sikkit, al-Mutarrizi, al-Tha'alibi and others among the lexicographers said: "basmala the man," when he says "bismillah." It is said: "You have much basmalah," meaning much saying "bismillah." Similar to it: hawqala (he said: "la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah"), hallala (he said: "la ilaha illa Allah"), sabhala (he said: "subhan Allah"), hamdala (he said: "al-hamdu lillah"), haysala (he said: "hayya 'ala al-salah"), ja'fala (he said: "ju'iltu fidaka"), tabqala (he said: "atala Allah baqa'aka"), damd'aza (he said: "adama Allah 'izzaka"), and haifala (he said: "hayya 'ala al-falah"). Al-Mutarrizi did not mention haysalah (when he says "hayya 'ala al-salah"), ja'fala (when he says "ju'iltu fidaka"), tabqala (when he says "atala Allah baqa'aka"), or damd'aza (when he says "adama Allah 'izzaka").

Eighth: The Shari'ah recommends mentioning the basmalah at the beginning of every action, such as eating, drinking, slaughtering, intercourse, purification, boarding a ship, and other actions. God the Exalted said: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾ ... ﴿And He said: Embark therein; in the name of God is its course and its anchoring﴾. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Close your door and mention the name of God; extinguish your lamp and mention the name of God; cover (khammir) your vessel and mention the name of God; tie the mouth of your water-skin (awka siqa'aka) and mention the name of God." [[Al-tahmir: covering. Al-wika': the cord with which the bag or purse and other things are tied. That is, tie the mouths of the water-skins with the wika' so that no animal enters them or anything falls into them.]] He also said: "If one of you, when he wishes to approach his wife, says: 'In the name of God. O God, keep Satan away from us and keep Satan away from what You provide us,' then if a child is decreed between them, Satan will never harm it." He said to Umar ibn Abi Salamah: "O boy, mention the name of God, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is near you." And he said: "Indeed Satan considers food lawful unless the name of God is mentioned over it." And he said: "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of God." Uthman ibn Abi al-As complained to him of a pain he had felt in his body since he embraced Islam, and the Messenger of God ﷺ said to him: "Place your hand on the part of your body where you feel pain, and say 'bismillah' three times, and say seven times: 'I seek refuge in the might of God and His power from the evil of what I find and fear.'" All of this is established in the Sahih. Ibn Majah and al-Tirmidhi narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The screen between the jinn and the private parts of the children of Adam, when one enters the privy, is that he says 'bismillah'." Al-Daraqutni narrated from Aisha, who said: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ touched his water for purification, he would mention the name of God the Exalted, then pour water over his hands."

Ninth: Our scholars said: In this there is a refutation of the Qadariyyah and others who say that their actions are within their own power. The basis of the argument against them from this is that God, glory be to Him, commanded us, at the beginning of every action, to open it with this, as we have mentioned. The meaning of ﴿bismillah﴾ is: "with God." And the meaning of "with God" is: by His creation and His decree, one reaches what one reaches. More explanation of this will come, if God the Exalted wills.

Some of them said: the meaning of His saying ﴿bismillah﴾ is: "I begin with the help, the success and the blessing of God." This is an instruction from God the Exalted to His servants, that they should mention His name at the beginning of recitation and other things, so that the beginning is with the blessing of God, Majestic and Mighty.

Tenth: Abu Ubayd Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna held that "ism" (name) is an extra, redundant particle, and he cited the verse of Labid:
"Until the year is complete, then the greeting of peace upon you both; / and whoever weeps a full year has surely made an excuse."
Here he mentioned "ism" as an addition, when he meant only: "then the greeting of peace upon you both." Our scholars have used this verse of Labid to establish that the name is the named (al-ism huwa al-musamma). The discussion of this will come in this chapter and elsewhere, if God the Exalted wills.

Eleventh: There is disagreement about the meaning of the addition of "ism." Qutrub said: it was added to magnify the mention of Him, the Exalted, and to exalt Him. Al-Akhfash said: it was added so that by mentioning it, the expression would move from the ruling of an oath to the intention of seeking blessing, because the original sentence is: "billah."

Twelfth: They also differed concerning the meaning of the entry of the letter "ba'" upon it: did it enter with the sense of a command, with the implied meaning: "Begin with the name of God"? Or with the sense of a statement, with the implied meaning: "I have begun with the name of God"? There are two views: the first is that of the reciters (qurra'), and the second that of al-Zajjaj. So "bismillah" is in the accusative position according to both interpretations. It was also said: the meaning is "my beginning is with the name of God," so "bismillah" is in the nominative position as the predicate of the subject. It was also said: the predicate is omitted, meaning "my beginning is established or fixed with the name of God," so when you make it explicit, "bismillah" is in the accusative position with "established" or "fixed," and it is like your saying: "Zayd is in the house." In revelation: ﴿So when he saw it settled with him, he said: This is of the favour of my Lord﴾, where "indahu" (with him) is in the accusative position. This was related from the grammarians of Basrah. It was also said: the meaning is "my beginning with the name of God is present or established," so "bi-ismi" is in the accusative position by the verbal noun which is "ibtida'i" (my beginning).

Thirteenth: "Bismillah" is written without an alif, being dispensed with the alif by the attached ba' (ba' al-ilsaq) in pronunciation and in writing, because of its frequent use. This is unlike His saying: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾, for there the alif is deleted because of its infrequent use. They differed about deleting it with "al-Rahman" and "al-Qahir." Al-Kisa'i and Sa'id al-Akhfash said: the alif is deleted. Yahya ibn Wathhab said: it is not deleted except with "bismillah" only, because it is only in this that usage has become frequent.

Fourteenth: They also differed about the specification of the ba' of genitive (ba' al-jarr) being kasrah, on three meanings. It was said: so that its pronunciation would match its function. It was also said: since the ba' only enters upon nouns, it was specified with the jarr that occurs only with nouns. Third: to distinguish it from letters that may sometimes be nouns, such as the kaf in the saying of the poet [[He is Imru' al-Qays. The full verse and its explanation will come on p. 211 of this part.]]:
"And we went out with one like the son of the water, who is pulled through the middle of us,"
meaning: with the like of the son of the water, or whatever is like it.

Fifteenth: "Ism" (name) has the form af'un (or fi'l/fu'l), its omitted letter is the waw, because it is from "sumtu" (I rose/elevated), its plural is asma', and its diminutive is sumayy. There is disagreement about the original form: it was said: fi'l, and it was said: fu'l. Al-Jawhari said: asma' may be a plural of this pattern, as in jidh/ajdha' and qufl/aqfal, and this form is known only by hearing. It has four dialect forms: ism with kasrah, usm with dammah. Ahmad ibn Yahya said: whoever takes the alif with dammah derives it from "sumtu asmu," and whoever takes it with kasrah derives it from "sumtu asma." It is also said: sim and sum, and it is recited in verse:
"And God has named you with a blessed name, by which God has preferred you with preference."
Another said:
"Our year, its arrival pleased us, called Abu al-Samh; and Qurdhab is its name / a man who leans upon things, salting them, stripping the flesh from every bone." [[Mubtarak: a man who leans on a thing and is salted. Yalhamuh: strips the flesh from it.]]
Qarda'a the man: when he eats something dry, he is qirdhab. "Simuh" with dammah and kasrah both. From it is the saying of the other:
"In the name of Him who in every surah is its name" (simuh).
The sin in "bism" became quiescent by irregular derivation [[The original was "ism," the hamzah's vowel was moved to the sin, then the hamzah was deleted; and when the ba' joined it, the sin became quiescent for lightness.]], not by analogy, and its alif is an alif of connection (alif wasl). Sometimes the poet makes it an alif of cutting (qat') out of necessity, as in the saying of al-Ahwas:
"And I am not one despised among the lineage of Malik, nor one who calls himself by a name and then does not fulfil what is named." [[Al-makhsus: the despised. Jidhm of everything: its root. Malik: the poet's great-grandfather.]]

**The sixteenth point:** The Arabs, in forming the relative adjective from *ism* (name), say *samawiyy*, and some say *ismiyy*, leaving it in its original state. Its plural is *asma'*, and the plural of *asma'* is *asami*. Al-Farra' transmitted: "I seek refuge for you in the names (*asma'*) of God."

**The seventeenth point:** Scholars disagreed about the derivation of *ism* (name), in two ways. The Basrans said it is derived from *sumuw*, meaning height and elevation. It was said that it is called *ism* because its bearer is in the position of one who is raised by it. It was also said that the name rises (*yasmu*) by means of the named thing and elevates it above others. And it was said that *ism* was named *ism* because it rises, by its strength, above the two divisions of speech, the particle (*harf*) and the verb (*fi'l*). The noun (*ism*) is by consensus stronger than both, because it is the basis, so it was named *ism* for its elevation over them. These are three opinions. The Kufans said that it is derived from *simah*, meaning a mark or sign, because the name is a sign for the one it was assigned to. On this view, the root of *ism* is *wasama*. The first view is more correct, because in the diminutive one says *sumayy*, and in the plural *asma'*. The plural and the diminutive return things to their roots, so one does not say *wasim* or *awsam*. What also supports the first view is the practical difference it makes, which is:

**The eighteenth point:** Whoever holds that *ism* is derived from elevation says that God, glory be to Him, has always been described before the creation of creatures, after their existence, and at their passing away, and that they have no effect on His names or attributes. This is the position of the People of the Sunna (*Ahl al-Sunna*, the orthodox majority). Whoever holds that *ism* is derived from *simah* says that God was, in pre-eternity, without name or attribute; then when He created creatures, they gave Him names and attributes; and when He annihilates them, He will remain without name or attribute. This is the position of the Mu'tazila (rationalist sect), and it contradicts what the community (*ummah*) has agreed upon. It is a greater error than their saying that His speech is created. Exalted is God above that!

On this disagreement the discussion of the name and the named (*al-ism wa'l-musamma*) also arises, which is:

**The nineteenth point:** The people of truth, according to what al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib transmitted, hold that the name is the named itself. Ibn Furak endorsed this, and it is the view of Abu 'Ubayda and Sibawayh. When someone says, "God is Knowing," his statement indicates the Essence described as knowing; so the name is His being knowing, and this is the named itself. Likewise, when he says, "God is Creator," the Creator is the Lord, and this is precisely the name. So for them the name is the named itself, without distinction.

Ibn al-Hassar said: Those innovators who deny the attributes claim that the designations (*tasmiyat*) signify nothing but the Essence. For this reason they say the name is other than the named. Whoever affirms the attributes affirms that the designations signify meanings which are descriptions of the Essence, and which are other than the expressions (*'ibarat*); these, in their view, are the names. Further explanation of this will come in *al-Baqara* and *al-A'raf*, God willing.

**The twentieth point:** His saying, "God" (*Allah*). This is the greatest of His names, glory be to Him, and the most comprehensive of them. Some scholars said it is the Greatest Name of God, and that no one else has been given it as a name. For this reason it is not made dual or plural. This is one of two interpretations of His saying: ﴿Do you know of any namesake for Him?﴾ (19:65), that is, anyone named with His name which is "Allah." So *Allah* is the name for the existing Truth, which comprises the attributes of divinity, which is described with the qualities of lordship, which alone possesses real existence, there is no god but Him, glory be to Him. It was said: its meaning is the One deserving of worship. It was said: its meaning is the Necessarily Existent, who has always been and always will be. The meanings are one.

**The twenty-first point:** They disagreed over whether this name is derived or is a proper noun assigned to the Essence. Many scholars took the first view. They disagreed about its derivation and root. Sibawayh transmitted from al-Khalil that its root is *ilah*, on the pattern of *fi'al*, and the *alif* and *lam* were introduced in place of the hamza. Sibawayh said: like *al-nas* whose root is *unas*. It was also said that the root of the word is *lah*, and on this the *alif* and *lam* entered for glorification; this is Sibawayh's own choice. He recited:

*By the Lah, your paternal cousin, you have not surpassed me in lineage,*
*nor are you my governor, so that you rule (*takhzuni*) me.*

The reading is *fa-takhzuni*, with the *kha'* dotted, and its meaning is "you govern me."

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the meaning of "bismillah" is "bism al-ilah." They removed the hamza, and assimilated the first *lam* into the second, so they became one doubled *lam*, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿But as for me, He is God, my Lord﴾ (18:38). Its meaning is *lakinna ana* ("but I"). Thus al-Hasan read it.

Then it was said: it is derived from *walaha*, meaning to be bewildered, and *al-walah* is the departure of reason. One says, "a man *walih*," and a woman *walihah* or *walih*, and *ma' mawlah* is water sent into the deserts. [Footnote in the source: "*Ma' mawlah*: pronounced with a damma on the *mim*, lightened *lam*, and the *waw* is either stressed or given a fatha."] So God, glory be to Him, is the one before whom minds are bewildered and lose themselves in the realities of His attributes and in thought about knowing Him. On this view the root of *ilah* and *lah* is the same, and the hamza is substituted for a *waw*, as it was in *ishah* and *wishah* and *isadah* and *wisadah*. This is transmitted from al-Khalil. It is also transmitted from al-Dahhak that he said: God was named *ilah* because creatures turn to Him (*yata'allahuna*) in their needs and humble themselves before Him in their hardships. It is reported from al-Khalil ibn Ahmad that he said: because creatures *ya'lahuna* to Him (with a fatha on the *lam*) and also *ya'lihuna* (with a kasra), and both are dialects. It was also said that it is derived from elevation. The Arabs used to say of everything elevated, "*lah*," so when the sun rose they would say, "*lahat*." It was said: it is derived from *alaha al-rajul*, when a man devoted himself to worship (*tanassaka*). From this is His saying: ﴿and your worship (*ilahataka*)﴾ (7:127), according to this reading. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: "and your worship." They said: so the name Allah is derived from this, and God, glory be to Him, means the one intended for worship. From this is the saying of the monotheists: "There is no god but God," meaning there is no one worshipped except God. The "*illa*" in the formula means "other than," not "except" in the sense of exception.

Some claimed that the original element in it is the *ha'* which is the pronoun for the absent, because they established Him in the innate disposition of their minds and pointed to Him with the pronominal particle. Then the *lam* of possession was added to it, since they knew that He is the Creator and Owner of things, so it became *lahu* ("to Him"). Then the *alif* and *lam* were added to it for glorification and exaltation.

*The second view:* This was held by a group of scholars too, including al-Shafi'i, Abu'l-Ma'ali, al-Khattabi, al-Ghazali, al-Mufaddal and others, and it was transmitted from al-Khalil and Sibawayh: that the *alif* and *lam* are inseparable from it, and it is not permissible to remove them. Al-Khattabi said: The proof that the *alif* and *lam* are part of the structure of this name, and were not added for definiteness, is that you do not say "*ya al-Rahman*" nor "*ya al-Rahim*," as you say "*ya Allah*." This shows that they are part of the form of the name. And God knows best.

**The twenty-second point:** They also disagreed about the derivation of His name *al-Rahman*. Some said: it has no derivation, because it is one of the names specific to Him, glory be to Him. Also, if it were derived from *rahmah* (mercy), it would not be joined with mention of the one shown mercy. It would then be permissible to say "God is *Rahman* to His servants," just as one says "*Rahim* to His servants." Also, if it were derived from *rahmah*, the Arabs would not have rejected it when they heard it, since they did not deny the mercy of their Lord. God, Mighty and Majestic, has said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate yourselves to the Merciful," they say, "And what is the Merciful?"﴾ (25:60), and so on.

When 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, wrote in the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya, by the Prophet's command, "In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate," Suhayl ibn 'Amr said: "As for 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate,' we do not know what 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate' is! Rather, write what we know: 'In Your name, O God,'" and the hadith continues.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: They were ignorant only of the attribute, not of the One described. He supported this with their saying "*wa ma al-Rahman*" ("And what is the Merciful?") and not "*wa man al-Rahman*" ("And who is the Merciful?"). Ibn al-Hassar said: It seems that he, may God have mercy on him, did not read the other verse: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Merciful﴾ (13:30).

The majority of people held that *al-Rahman* is derived from *rahmah* and built for intensity. Its meaning is the Possessor of mercy who has no peer in it. For this reason it is not made dual or plural, as *al-Rahim* is made dual and plural. Ibn al-Hassar said: Among the things that indicate derivation is what al-Tirmidhi reported and graded authentic from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, that he heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "God, Mighty and Majestic, said: I am the Merciful. I created the womb and derived for it a name from My name. Whoever joins it, I join him; and whoever severs it, I sever him." This is an explicit text on derivation, so there is no sense in opposing it or dissenting from it. The Arabs' rejection of it was due to their ignorance of God and of what is due to Him.

**The twenty-third point:** Al-Mubarrad claimed, as reported by Ibn al-Anbari in his book *al-Zahir*, that *al-Rahman* is a Hebrew name, which is why it came together with *al-Rahim*. He recited:

*You will not attain glory, nor will you wrap your cloaks in silk, nor make the* yanbut *(a kind of tree) into your fleece,*
*nor will you leave your migration to al-Qassayn, nor will you wipe their backs as a Merciful offering (*rahman qurbanan*).*

(The poem is by Jarir; *yanbut* is a kind of tree.) Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said in *Ma'ani al-Qur'an*: Ahmad ibn Yahya said: "*al-Rahim*" is Arabic and "*al-Rahman*" is Hebrew, so He joined them together. This view is rejected. Abu'l-Abbas said: An epithet may be used for praise, as you say, "Jarir the poet said." Mutarrif reported from Qatada concerning His saying: ﴿In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate﴾, that he said: "He praised Himself." Abu Ishaq said: This is a good view. Qutrub said: It is possible that He joined them together for emphasis. Abu Ishaq said: This is a good view, and emphasis has great benefit, and it is common in Arabic speech and needs no citation. The benefit of this, as Muhammad ibn Yazid said, is: a favor upon a favor, a bounty upon a bounty, a strengthening of the hopes of those who desire, and a promise that does not disappoint the one who hopes.

**The twenty-fourth point:** They disagreed whether the two have one meaning or two meanings. It was said: they have one meaning, like *nadman* and *nadim* (both meaning "companion"). This was said by Abu 'Ubayda. It was also said: the pattern *fa'lan* is not like *fa'il*, because *fa'lan* is used only for intensification of the action, as in your saying, "a *ghadban* man" ("a man filled with anger"), while *fa'il* may be in the sense of the active or passive participle. 'Amallas said:

*But when war bites you with a bite, you are the one who is turned toward and compassionate (*rahim*).*

**Tafsir Surah al-Fatihah** (exegesis of the Chapter of the Opening)
*(By the power and generosity of Allah)*

In it there are four sections:

The first section concerns its virtues and names, and it contains seven issues.

Al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, on Surah 1, verse 1 (part 4 of 10):

"Al-Rahman" is specific in its name but general in its action, and "al-Rahim" is general in its name but specific in its action. This is the view of the majority. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "Al-Rahman" is a name general to all kinds of mercy, and it is exclusive to Allah. "Al-Rahim" applies only to the believers, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and He is ever Merciful to the believers﴾.

Al-'Arzami [[He is 'Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman al-'Arzami, as in al-Khulasa.]] said: "Al-Rahman" is merciful to all His creation in the cities, through the blessings of the senses and the general blessings, and "al-Rahim" is merciful to the believers by guiding them and showing them gentleness.

Ibn al-Mubarak said: "Al-Rahman," when asked, gives; "al-Rahim," when not asked, becomes angry.

Ibn Majah in his *Sunan* and al-Tirmidhi in his *Jami'* narrated from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does not ask Allah, He becomes angry with him." This is the wording of al-Tirmidhi. Ibn Majah's wording is: "Whoever does not call upon Allah, glorified is He, He becomes angry with him."

He [al-Tirmidhi] said: I asked Abu Zur'ah about this Abu Salih, and he said: He is the one called al-Farisi, and he is Khuzi [[Relating to Khuzistan, a region between Persia and Basra.]], and I do not know his name.

Some poets took up this meaning and said:
*Allah becomes angry if you abandon asking Him,*
*while the son of Adam, when asked, becomes angry.*

Ibn 'Abbas said: They are two tender names, one of them more tender than the other, meaning more merciful.

Al-Khattabi said: This is problematic, because tenderness has no place in any of the attributes of Allah, may He be exalted.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl al-Bajali said: This is an error of the narrator, because tenderness is not among the attributes of Allah at all. Rather, they are two gentle names, one of them gentler than the other, and gentleness (*rifq*) is one of the attributes of Allah, may He be mighty and majestic. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah is Gentle (*rafiq*) and loves gentleness, and He gives for gentleness what He does not give for harshness."

**The twenty-fifth issue:** Most scholars hold that "al-Rahman" is exclusive to Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, and it is not permissible for anyone else to be named by it. Do you not see that He said: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful﴾? So He equated it with the name that no one else shares. And He said: ﴿Ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Did We appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Merciful?﴾ So He informed that "al-Rahman" is the one deserving of worship, glorified and exalted is He.

Musaylimah al-Kadhdhab, may Allah curse him, dared to name himself "Rahman of Yamamah," but he did not take that name until the description of "the liar" reached his ears, so Allah imposed on him the description of "the liar" because of that. Although every disbeliever is a liar, this attribute became for Musaylimah a label by which he is known, which Allah imposed upon him.

It has been said about the name "al-Rahman" that it is the Greatest Name of Allah. This was mentioned by Ibn al-'Arabi.

**The twenty-sixth issue:** "Al-Rahim" is an attribute of created beings. Because "al-Rahman" includes generality, it is placed before "al-Rahim" in our speech, in agreement with the revelation. This was said by al-Mahdawi.

It has also been said that the meaning of "al-Rahim" is: "with the Merciful (*al-Rahim*) you reached Allah," so "al-Rahim" is the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), and Allah has described him with that, saying: ﴿Most kind and merciful﴾. The meaning then seems to be that he says: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful and the Merciful," meaning: "and through Muhammad (ﷺ) you reached Me," that is, by following him and what he brought, you reached My reward, My honour, and beholding My Face. And Allah knows best.

**The twenty-seventh issue:** It is reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, that he said regarding the words "In the name of Allah": it is a healing from every disease and an aid toward every remedy. As for "al-Rahman," it is an aid for everyone who believes in Him, and it is a name that He has not given to anyone else. As for "al-Rahim," it is for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds.

Some have interpreted it letter by letter. It is reported from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the explanation of "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Merciful," and he said: "As for the *ba'* (ب), it is the trial (*bala'*) of Allah, His refreshment, His radiance, and His splendour. As for the *sin* (س), it is the loftiness (*sana'*) of Allah. As for the *mim* (م), it is the kingdom (*mulk*) of Allah. As for Allah, there is no god but Him. As for al-Rahman, He is the one who inclines (*al-'atif*) toward the righteous and the wicked among His creation. As for al-Rahim, He is the gentle one (*al-rafiq*) toward the believers in particular."

It is also reported from Ka'b al-Ahbar that he said: The *ba'* is His splendour (*baha'*), and the *sin* is His loftiness (*sana'*), so nothing is higher than Him. The *mim* is His kingdom, and He is over all things powerful, so nothing can overpower Him.

It has also been said that each letter is the opening of one of His names. The *ba'* is the key to His name *Basir* (the All-Seeing), the *sin* is the key to His name *Sami'* (the All-Hearing), the *mim* is the key to His name *Malik* (the King), the *alif* is the key to His name *Allah*, the *lam* is the key to His name *Latif* (the Subtle), the *ha'* is the key to His name *Hadi* (the Guide), the *ra'* is the key to His name *Raziq* (the Provider), the *ha'* (ح) is the key to His name *Halim* (the Forbearing), and the *nun* is the key to His name *Nur* (the Light). The meaning of all this is calling upon Allah, exalted is He, at the beginning of everything.

**The twenty-eighth issue:** There is disagreement regarding joining "al-Rahim" with "Al-hamdu lillah" (All praise is due to Allah). It is reported from Umm Salamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "al-Rahim. Al-hamd" (with the *mim* of al-Rahim vowelled with a sukun, pausing on it, and beginning with a severed *alif*). Some of the Kufans recited this way. But the majority of people recited "al-Rahimi al-hamdu," making *al-Rahimi* in the genitive case and joining the *alif* of *al-hamdu*. Al-Kisa'i reported from some Arabs that it is recited "al-Rahima al-hamdu" with a fatha on the *mim* and joining the *alif*, as if the *mim* were vowelled with a sukun, the *alif* was severed, then its vowel was transferred onto the *mim* and the *alif* was dropped.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: As far as I know, this recitation has not been transmitted from anyone. This is the view of Yahya ibn Ziyad concerning the words of Allah, may He be exalted: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Allah﴾.

**First:** Abu Hurayrah... Actually, the text begins: Al-Tirmidhi related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah has not sent down in the Torah or in the Gospel anything like Umm al-Qur'an, and it is the seven oft-repeated (al-sab' al-mathani) and it is divided [[i.e., Allah said: it is divided]] between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks." Malik related from al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'qub: that Abu Sa'id, client of ['Abd Allah ibn] 'Amir ibn Kurayz, informed him that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called Ubayy ibn Ka'b while he was praying, and he mentioned the hadith. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Abu Sa'id is not identified by a known name, and he is counted among the people of Madina; his narration is from Abu Hurayrah, and this hadith is mursal. This hadith was also related from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, a man from the Companions whose name is likewise not known, and it was narrated from him by Hafs ibn 'Asim and 'Ubayd ibn Hunayn. I say: Thus he said in al-Tamhid: "He is not identified by a known name." He mentioned in the Kitab al-Sahaba the difference of opinion regarding his name. The hadith was recorded by al-Bukhari from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, who said: "I was praying in the mosque when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called me, and I did not answer him. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I was praying.' He said: 'Did Allah not say: ﴿O you who believe, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you﴾ [al-Anfal 8:24]?' Then he said: 'I will surely teach you a surah that is the greatest surah in the Qur'an before you leave the mosque.' Then he took my hand, and when he wanted to leave I said to him: 'Did you not say you would teach me the greatest surah in the Qur'an?' He said: '[Al-Hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin] is the seven oft-repeated and the Great Qur'an that I have been given.'" Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others said: Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla was among the eminent Ansar and their leaders. Al-Bukhari alone related it. His name is Rafi', and it is said: al-Harith ibn Nufay' ibn al-Mu'alla, and it is said: Aws ibn al-Mu'alla, and it is said: Abu Sa'id ibn Aws ibn al-Mu'alla. He died in the year seventy-four [AH] at the age of sixty-four [[Ibn Hajar said in al-Isaba: "This is an error, for it would imply that his story with the Prophet ﷺ occurred when he was a child, and the context of the hadith rejects that."]] years, and he was the first to pray facing the qibla when it was changed. (It will come later [[see vol. 2, p. 149]].) Yazid ibn Zuray' also transmitted the hadith of Ubayy: he said: Rawh ibn al-Qasim narrated to us from al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out to Ubayy while he was praying, and he mentioned the hadith in its meaning. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned in his book al-Radd [against him]: my father narrated to me, Abu 'Ubayd Allah al-Warraq narrated to me, Abu Dawud narrated to us, Shayban narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, who said: Iblis, may Allah curse him, cried out four cries: when he was cursed, when he was cast down from Paradise, when Muhammad ﷺ was sent, and when the Opening of the Book (Fatihat al-Kitab) was revealed. It was revealed in Madina.

**Second:** The scholars differed about whether some surahs and verses are superior to others, and whether some of Allah's Most Beautiful Names are superior to others. Some people said: there is no superiority of one over another, because all of it is the speech of Allah, and likewise His names have no comparison among them. This was the view of Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, the judge Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Hibban al-Busti, and a group of jurists. Its meaning is also related from Malik. Yahya ibn Yahya said: "Preferring some of the Qur'an over others is an error." Likewise Malik disliked that a surah be repeated or singled out to the exclusion of others. He also said, regarding the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:106], that he said: "It is muhkama (firm) in place of mansukha (abrogated)." Ibn Kinana related all of this from Malik. Those who held this view argued that: "Superiority implies the inferiority of the lesser, while the essence is one in everything, and it is the speech of Allah, and the speech of Allah has no deficiency." Al-Busti said: The meaning of this phrase ("Nothing in the Torah or the Gospel is like Umm al-Qur'an") is that Allah Most High does not give the reader of the Torah and the Gospel the same reward as He gives the reader of Umm al-Qur'an, since Allah, in His grace, favoured this Ummah over other nations, and gave it, for reciting His speech, more grace than He gave others for reciting His speech, and that is a grace from Him to this Ummah. He said: The meaning of his saying "the greatest surah" is intended in terms of reward, not that some of the Qur'an is superior to others. Others said that superiority is real, and that what is contained in the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿Your God is One God; there is no god but He, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:163], the Verse of the Throne (ayat al-kursi), the end of Surat al-Hashr, and Surat al-Ikhlas, of indications of His oneness and attributes, is not found in ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ [al-Masad 111:1] and what is like it. Superiority is only in the wondrous meanings and their abundance, not in terms of the attribute itself, and this is the truth. Among those who held superiority were Ishaq ibn Rahawayh [[Ibn Khallikan vocalized it: (with a fatha on the ra after the alif, then a silent ha, then a silent ta-like waw, then a silent ya beneath, then a silent ha; it was also said: Rahawayh, with a damma on the ha, a sukun on the waw, and a fatha on the ya.)]] and others among the scholars and theologians, and this is the choice of the judge Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi and Ibn al-Hassar, based on the hadith of Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla and the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, that he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: "O Ubayy, which verse in the Book of Allah is the greatest with you?" He said: I said: "Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting" [al-Baqarah 2:255]. He said: He struck my chest and said: "May knowledge be pleasant for you, O Abu al-Mundhir." Recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim. Ibn al-Hassar said: "I am amazed at one who mentions disagreement in the face of these texts." Ibn al-'Arabi said: His saying "Nothing in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Qur'an is like it" leaves aside the rest of the books, such as the scrolls that were sent down, the Psalms and others, because what is mentioned is the best of them; and when a thing is the best of the best, it becomes the best of all, as when you say: "Zayd is the best of scholars, so he is the best of people." In al-Fatiha are attributes that are not found in others, to the extent that it was said: the whole Qur'an is in it. It is twenty-five words that comprise all the sciences of the Qur'an. Among its excellences is that Allah, glorified is He, divided it between Himself and His servant; no act of worship is valid without it, and no deed attains its reward (without it). In this sense it became Umm al-Qur'an al-'Azim, just as ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ [al-Ikhlas 112:1] is equal to a third of the Qur'an, since the Qur'an is monotheism, legislation and admonition, and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ contains all of monotheism. In this sense was the clarification in his ﷺ saying to Ubayy: "Which verse in the Qur'an is the greatest?" He said: "Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting." It was the greatest verse only because it is entirely monotheism, just as his saying: "The best thing I and the prophets before me have said is: There is no god but Allah, alone, without partner" became the best of remembrance, because these are words that contain all the knowledge of monotheism, and al-Fatiha includes monotheism, worship, admonition and reminder. This is not far-fetched for the power of Allah Most High.

**Third:** Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) related: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Opening of the Book, the Verse of the Throne, ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:18], and ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:26], these verses are suspended from the Throne; there is no veil between them and Allah." Abu 'Amr al-Dani supported it with a chain in his book al-Bayan.

**Fourth:** On its names: they are twelve.

**The first:** al-Salat (the Prayer) [[In the tafsir of al-Alusi and others: "Surat al-Salat."]]. Allah Most High said [[i.e., in the hadith qudsi]]: "I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves," the hadith... which has already passed.

**The second:** [Surah] al-Hamd (the Praise), because it contains the mention of praise, as one says: Surat al-A'raf, al-Anfal, al-Tawba, and the like.

**The third:** Fatihat al-Kitab (the Opening of the Book), without any disagreement among the scholars. It was named so because the recitation of the Qur'an begins with it verbally, the writing in the Mushaf begins with it in script, and the prayers begin with it.

**The fourth:** Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book). On this name there is disagreement. The majority permitted it, while Anas, al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin disliked it. Al-Hasan said: "Umm al-Kitab is the lawful and the unlawful," for Allah Most High said: ﴿They are the foundation of the Book, and others are ambiguous﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:7]. Anas and Ibn Sirin said: "Umm al-Kitab is the name of the Preserved Tablet." Allah Most High said: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:4].

**The fifth:** Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an). This too is disputed: the majority permitted it, while Anas and Ibn Sirin disliked it, but the established hadiths refute these two views. Al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Al-Hamdu lillah is Umm al-Qur'an, Umm al-Kitab, and the seven oft-repeated." He said: This is a hadith that is hasan sahih. In al-Bukhari he said: "It was named Umm al-Kitab because writing it in the Mushafs begins with it, and recitation of it in the prayer begins with it." Yahya ibn Ya'mur said: "Umm al-Qura is Makka, Umm Khurasan is Marw, and Umm al-Qur'an is Surat al-Hamd." It was said: It was named Umm al-Qur'an because it is the beginning of it and includes all its sciences, and by this Makka was named Umm al-Qura because it is the first of the earth, and from it the earth was spread out. From this also a mother (umm) is called umm because she is the origin of offspring, and the earth is called umm, in the saying of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

*The earth is our refuge, and it was our mother;*
*in it are our graves, and in it we are born.*

A battle standard is called umm because it goes before and the army follows it. The root of umm is ummah, and for this reason it is pluralized as ummahat, as Allah Most High said: ﴿And your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:23]. It is also said ummat without the ha, as he said: *You dispelled the darkness with your mothers (ummatika).* It was also said: ummahat is used for people, and ummat for animals, related by Ibn Faris in al-Mujmal.

**The sixth:** al-Mathani (the oft-repeated). It was named so because it is repeated in every rak'ah. It was also said: it was named so because it was set apart (istuthniyat) for this Ummah, so it was not sent down to anyone before it, as a treasure for it.

**The seventh:** al-Qur'an al-'Azim (the Great Qur'an). It was named so because it includes all the sciences of the Qur'an, for it comprises praise of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with the attributes of His perfection and majesty; a command to acts of worship and sincerity in them; acknowledgment of incapacity to perform any of them except by His help; supplication to Him for guidance to the Straight Path, and sufficiency against the affairs of those who break faith; and it indicates the end of those who deny.

**The eighth:** al-Shifa' (the Healing). Al-Darimi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Opening of the Book is a cure for every poison" [[What is in the Musnad of al-Darimi, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr: he said: The Messenger of Allah (said: "In the Opening of the Book is a cure for every disease.")]].

**The ninth:** al-Ruqyah (the incantation). This is established from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the man who performed the incantation over the chief of the tribe: "What made you know that it is an incantation?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, something was cast into my heart," and the hadith... The imams recorded it, and it will come in full.

**(The tenth)**: *al-Asās* (the foundation). A man complained to al-Sha'bi of pain in his side, and he said: "Hold to the *asās* of the Qur'an, the Opening (*Fātiḥat al-Kitāb*). I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: Every thing has a foundation (*asās*). The foundation of the world is Makkah, because the earth was spread out from it. The foundation of the heavens is *'Arībā*, which is the seventh heaven. [[In some copies: *gharībā* (with the dotted ghayn).]] The foundation of the earth is *'Ajībā*, which is the seventh and lowest earth. The foundation of the gardens is the Garden of Eden, which is the navel of the gardens, upon which the Garden was founded. The foundation of the Fire is Jahannam, which is the seventh and lowest level, upon which the levels were founded. The foundation of creation is Adam, the foundation of the prophets is Noah, the foundation of the Children of Israel is Jacob, the foundation of the Books is the Qur'an, the foundation of the Qur'an is the Fātiḥah, and the foundation of the Fātiḥah is *Bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm*. So if you are ill or in pain, then hold to the Fātiḥah and you will be healed." [[Thus in all copies of the original. Had it been a response to the imperative, it would read *tashfi* in the jussive (*tushfa* → *tashfi*).]]

**(The eleventh)**: *al-Wāfiyah* (the complete one). This was said by Sufyān ibn 'Uyaynah, because it cannot be divided into halves and does not admit of abridgement. If one recites half of another sūrah in one rak'ah and the other half in another rak'ah, it suffices; but if the Fātiḥah is divided between two rak'ahs, it does not suffice.

**(The twelfth)**: *al-Kāfiyah* (the sufficient one). Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr said: "Because it suffices in place of others, and others do not suffice in its place." This is supported by what Muḥammad ibn Khallād al-Iskandarānī narrated, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Umm al-Qur'an is a substitute for other than it, and nothing other than it is a substitute for it."

**The fifth**: al-Muhallab said: "The place of the healing (*ruqyah*) in it is only: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fātiḥah 1:5]." It was also said: "The whole sūrah is a healing (*ruqyah*), because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to the man when he informed him: 'And how do you know that it is a *ruqyah*?' He did not say: 'that in it there is a *ruqyah*.' This indicates that the whole sūrah is a *ruqyah*, because it is the opening of the Book and its beginning, and it contains all of its sciences, as has been mentioned earlier. And Allah knows best."

**The sixth**: The naming of it as *al-Mathānī* (the oft-repeated) and *Umm al-Kitāb* (the Mother of the Book) does not prevent other things from being named thus. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿A Book, consistent, oft-repeated (*mathānī*)﴾ [al-Zumar 39:23]. So He applied *mathānī* to His Book, because the reports are repeated in it. The seven long (*al-sab' al-ṭiwāl*) have also been called *mathānī*, because the obligations and the stories are repeated in them. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given seven of the *mathānī*." He said: "The seven long ones." This was recorded by al-Nasā'ī. From al-Baqarah to al-A'rāf there are six, and they differed about the seventh. It was said: Yūnus. It was said: al-Anfāl and al-Tawbah, and this is the view of Mujāhid and Sa'īd ibn Jubayr. And the poet A'shā Hamdān said:

*"So crowd the mosque and call upon your Lord,*
*and study these, the mathānī and the ṭiwāl."*

More explanation of this will come in the sūrah of al-Ḥijr, Allah willing. [[See vol. 15, p. 249.]]

**The seventh**: *al-Mathānī* is the plural of *mathnā*, which is that which comes after the first. *Al-Ṭiwal* is the plural of *aṭwal*. Al-Anfāl has been called *mathānī* because it follows the long ones in length. It was also said: they are the sūrahs whose verses exceed the *mufaṣṣal* and fall short of the *mi'īn*. The *mi'ūn* are the sūrahs each of which exceeds one hundred verses.

**Second section: on its revelation and its rulings**, containing twenty issues.

**The first**: The *ummah* has reached consensus (*ijmā'*) that the Opening of the Book (*Fātiḥat al-Kitāb*) has seven verses, except what is narrated from Ḥusayn al-Ju'fī, that it has six, and this is an anomalous (*shādh*) view. And except what is narrated from 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, that he counted ﴿You alone we worship﴾ as a verse, making it eight verses, and this too is anomalous. The saying of the Most High: ﴿And We have given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ [al-Ḥijr 15:87], and His saying (in the ḥadīth): "I have divided the prayer..." refute these two views. The *ummah* has also reached consensus that it is part of the Qur'an. If it is asked: "If it were Qur'an, Ibn Mas'ūd would have included it in his codex (*muṣḥaf*); since he did not include it, this shows that it is not part of the Qur'an, like the two *mu'awwidhatān* in his view." The answer is what Abū Bakr al-Anbārī mentioned. He said: Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥubāb narrated to us, Sulaymān ibn al-Ash'ath narrated to us, Ibn Abī Qudāmah narrated to us, Jarīr narrated to us from al-A'mash, who said: "I think he related it from Ibrāhīm, who said: It was said to 'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd: 'Why did you not write the Opening of the Book in your codex?' He said: 'If I had written it, I would have had to write it with every sūrah.'" Abū Bakr said: He means that every rak'ah must begin with *Umm al-Qur'an* before the sūrah recited after it. So he said: "I abbreviated by omitting it, and I trusted in the Muslims' memorization of it, and I did not include it in a place where I would be obliged to write it with every sūrah, since it precedes them in the prayer."

**The second**: They differed over whether it is Makkan or Madinan. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatādah, Abū al-'Āliyah al-Riyāḥī (whose name is Rufay') and others said: it is Makkan. Abū Hurayrah, Mujāhid, 'Aṭā' ibn Yasār, al-Zuhrī and others said: it is Madinan. It is also said: half of it was revealed in Makkah and half in Madinah. This was transmitted by Abū al-Layth Naṣr ibn Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Samarqandī in his *tafsīr*. The first view is more correct, because of the saying of the Most High: ﴿And We have given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the Great Qur'an﴾ [al-Ḥijr 15:87], and al-Ḥijr is Makkan by consensus. There is no disagreement that the obligation of the prayer was in Makkah. And it is not known that a prayer was ever performed in Islam without ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. This is indicated by his saying (ﷺ): "There is no prayer except with the Opening of the Book." This is a report about the ruling, not about the beginning. And Allah knows best.

Al-Qāḍī Ibn al-Ṭayyib has mentioned the people's disagreement about what was first revealed of the Qur'an. It was said: al-Muddaththir; it was said: *Iqra'*; it was said: the Fātiḥah. Al-Bayhaqī mentioned in *Dalā'il al-Nubuwwah* from Abū Maysarah 'Amr ibn Shuraḥbīl that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Khadījah: "When I am alone by myself I hear a call, and by Allah I have feared that this is a matter..." She said: "Never! Allah would not do that to you. By Allah, you fulfil trusts, you uphold kinship ties, and you speak the truth." When Abū Bakr entered, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was not there, Khadījah mentioned his account to him. She said: "O 'Atīq, go with Muḥammad to Waraqah ibn Nawfal." When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered, Abū Bakr took his hand and said: "Come with us to Waraqah." He said: "Who told you?" He said: "Khadījah." So they went to him and related it to him. He said: "When I am alone by myself, I hear a call behind me: 'O Muḥammad, O Muḥammad!' so I run off in fright into the earth." He said: "Do not do that. When it comes to you, stand firm until you hear what it says, then come to me and inform me." When he was alone, it called to him: "O Muḥammad, say: *In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds*, until it reached *nor of those who are astray*. Say: There is no god but Allah." He came to Waraqah and told him that. Waraqah said to him: "Rejoice, then rejoice! I bear witness that you are the one whom 'Īsā ibn Maryam gave good tidings of, that you are upon the like of the Law (*nāmūs*) of Mūsā, that you are a messenger sent, and that you will be commanded to fight after this day of yours, and if I live to see that, I will certainly fight alongside you." When Waraqah died, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have seen the priest (*al-qass*) in Paradise, wearing garments of silk, because he believed in me and affirmed me," meaning Waraqah. Al-Bayhaqī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "This is *munqaṭi'* (disconnected)," meaning this ḥadīth. If it is preserved, it may be a report about its revelation after the revelation of ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-'Alaq 96:1] and ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:1].

**The third**: Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: Some scholars thought that Jibrīl (peace be upon him) did not descend with the sūrah of al-Ḥamd, because of what Muslim related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "While Jibrīl was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ), he heard a *naqīḍ* [[*al-naqīḍ*: the sound.]] from above him. He raised his head and said: 'This is a gate from the heaven that has been opened today, which has never been opened except today.' So an angel descended from it and said: 'This is an angel who has descended to the earth, who has never descended except today.' He greeted and said: 'Rejoice in two lights that you have been given, which no prophet before you was given: the Opening of the Book and the closing verses of al-Baqarah. You will not recite a letter of them except that you will be given it.'" Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: "It is not as he thought, for this ḥadīth indicates that Jibrīl (peace be upon him) preceded the angel to the Prophet (ﷺ), informing him of it and of what would descend with it. On this view Jibrīl shared in its descent. And Allah knows best."

I say: The apparent meaning of the ḥadīth indicates that Jibrīl (peace be upon him) did not inform the Prophet (ﷺ) of anything of that. We have explained that its descent was in Makkah, and Jibrīl (peace be upon him) descended with it, because of the saying of the Most High: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has descended with it﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 26:193], and this implies the whole Qur'an. So Jibrīl (peace be upon him) descended with its recitation in Makkah, and the angel descended with its reward in Madinah. And Allah knows best. It has also been said that it is both Makkan and Madinan: Jibrīl descended with it twice, transmitted by al-Tha'labī. But what we have mentioned is preferable, for it combines the Qur'an and the Sunnah. And to Allah belongs the praise and the favour.

**The Fourth Issue:** It has already been established that, according to the sound opinion, the basmalah (the phrase "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate") is not a verse of the Fatihah. Given that, the ruling for one praying who has said the opening takbir (saying "Allahu akbar") is that he should connect it directly to the Fatihah without pausing, and should not recite any tawjih (the opening supplication beginning "I have turned my face...") or tasbih (glorification of God), because of the hadiths of 'A'ishah and Anas mentioned earlier and others. However, there are hadiths that mention the tawjih, the tasbih, and the pause, and a group of scholars has acted upon them. It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with them both, that when they began the prayer they would say: "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god besides You." This was also the view of Sufyan, Ahmad, Ishaq, and the Ashab al-Ra'y (the proponents of personal reasoning). Al-Shafi'i used to act upon what is narrated from 'Ali, from the Prophet ﷺ, that when he began the prayer he would say the takbir and then say: "I have turned my face..." — the full hadith, which Muslim transmitted, and which will come in full at the end of Surah al-An'am, where the discussion of this issue will be treated comprehensively, God willing. [See vol. 7, p. 153.]

Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is established that when the Messenger of God ﷺ said the takbir in the prayer, he would pause briefly before reciting, saying: "O God, place between me and my sins the distance You placed between the East and the West. O God, cleanse me of my sins as a white garment is cleansed of filth. O God, wash me of my sins with water, snow, and hail." Abu Hurayrah also practiced this. Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman said: "The imam has two pauses, so take advantage of them for recitation." Al-Awza'i, Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal inclined toward the Prophet's ﷺ hadith on this matter.

**The Fifth Issue:** The scholars differed regarding the obligation of reciting the Fatihah in the prayer. Malik and his companions said: it is specifically required for the imam and for one praying alone in every rak'ah (a unit of prayer). Ibn Khuwayz Mindad al-Basri al-Maliki said: There has been no difference in Malik's position that whoever forgets it in a rak'ah of a two-rak'ah prayer, his prayer is invalid and does not suffice him. His position differed regarding one who omits it forgetfully in one rak'ah of a four-rak'ah or three-rak'ah prayer: at one time he said he must repeat the prayer, and at another time he said he should perform the two prostrations of forgetfulness (sujud al-sahw). This is the narration of Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and others from Malik. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: It has also been said that he repeats that rak'ah and performs the prostrations of forgetfulness after the salam (the closing greeting). Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: The sound position is that that rak'ah is annulled and he performs another rak'ah in its place, like one who forgot to perform a prostration. This is the choice of Ibn al-Qasim.

Al-Hasan al-Basri, most of the people of Basra, and al-Mughirah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Makhzumi al-Madani said: If one recites Umm al-Qur'an (the Fatihah) once in the prayer, it suffices him and he does not need to repeat it, because it is a prayer in which he has recited Umm al-Qur'an, and it is complete, based on the Prophet's ﷺ saying, peace be upon him: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite Umm al-Qur'an," and this one has recited it. I say: It may be understood as "there is no prayer for one who does not recite it in every rak'ah," and this is the sound view, as will come. It may also be understood as "there is no prayer for one who does not recite it in the majority of the rak'ahs," and this is the cause of the disagreement, and God knows best.

Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri, and al-Awza'i said: If one deliberately omits it throughout his entire prayer and recites something else, it suffices him, though there is a difference of narration from al-Awza'i on this. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The minimum is three verses, or one long verse like the verse of debt. It is also narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan that he said: I permit personal judgment regarding the length of a verse and the length of an intelligible word, such as "al-hamdu lillah" (praise be to God), but I do not permit it for a single letter that does not constitute speech. Al-Tabari said: The one praying must recite Umm al-Qur'an in every rak'ah; if he does not recite it, it does not suffice him unless he recites the equivalent of it from the Qur'an in the number of its verses and letters. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: This has no meaning, because its specification and the explicit text concerning it have singled it out for this ruling to the exclusion of others, and it is impossible that one who is obligated to perform it, and abandons it while able to do so, should bring a substitute for it. Rather, he must bring it and return to it, like all other obligatory acts that are specifically required in worship.

**The Sixth Issue:** As for the follower (ma'mum), if he reaches the imam while he is in ruku' (bowing), the imam bears the recitation on his behalf, because of the consensus (ijma') that if he reaches the imam in ruku', he says the takbir, bows, and recites nothing. If he reaches the imam standing, then he recites.

**The Seventh Issue:** No one should abandon the recitation behind his imam in a silent prayer. If he does, he has done wrong, but there is no penalty for him according to Malik and his companions.

**The Eighth Issue:** As for when the imam recites aloud, according to the well-known position of Malik's school, there is no recitation of the Fatihah or of anything else, because of God's saying: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾ [al-A'raf: 204], the Messenger of God's ﷺ saying: "Why is it that I am being disputed with regarding the Qur'an?", his saying concerning the imam: "When he recites, be silent," and his saying: "Whoever has an imam, the imam's recitation is his recitation."

Al-Shafi'i, as transmitted from him by al-Buwayti, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: No one's prayer is valid unless he recites the Fatihah in every rak'ah, whether he is an imam or a follower, whether his imam recites aloud or silently. Al-Shafi'i, while in Iraq, used to say regarding the follower: he recites when the imam recites silently, and does not recite when the imam recites aloud, like the well-known position of Malik's school. In Egypt he said: Regarding the prayers in which the imam recites aloud, there are two views: one is that he should recite, and the other is that it suffices him not to recite and to rely on the imam's recitation. This was transmitted by Ibn al-Mundhir. Ibn Wahb, Ashhab, Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Ibn Habib, and the Kufans said: The follower recites nothing, whether his imam recites aloud or silently, because of the Prophet's ﷺ saying, peace be upon him: "The imam's recitation is his recitation," and this is general; and because of Jabir's saying: "Whoever prays a rak'ah in which he does not recite Umm al-Qur'an has not prayed except behind the imam."

**The Ninth Issue:** Of these positions, the sound one is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and the other view of Malik, namely that the Fatihah is specifically required in every rak'ah for everyone, in general, based on the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite in it the Opening of the Book (Fatihah al-Kitab)," and his saying: "Whoever prays a prayer in which he does not recite Umm al-Qur'an, it is khidaj (deficient)," three times. Abu Hurayrah said: The Messenger of God ﷺ commanded me to proclaim: "There is no prayer except with the recitation of the Opening of the Book and whatever is added to it," narrated by Abu Dawud. Just as the prostration or bowing of one rak'ah cannot substitute for that of another rak'ah, so too the recitation of one rak'ah cannot substitute for that of another. This was also the view of 'Abdullah ibn 'Awn, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Abu Thawr and others among the companions of al-Shafi'i, and Dawud ibn 'Ali. Something similar is narrated from al-Awza'i, and Makhul also held this view. It is also narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As, and Khawwat ibn Jubayr that they said: "There is no prayer except with the Opening of the Book." This is also the view of Ibn 'Umar, and the well-known position of al-Awza'i. These Companions are the exemplars and the models; all of them make the Fatihah obligatory in every rak'ah.

Abu 'Abdullah Muhammad ibn Yazid ibn Majah al-Qazwini, the imam, has transmitted in his Sunan what removes the disagreement and eliminates every

**[Continuing from a preceding discussion]** ... [the reasoning] "...doubt."
