He said: Abu Kurayb narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Fudayl; and Suwayd ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Ali ibn Mushhir; all of them from Abu Sufyan al-Sa'di, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite in every rak'ah the Opening of the Book (al-Hamdu lillah) and a surah, whether in an obligatory prayer or otherwise." In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, that he (upon him be peace) said to the man whom he taught the prayer: "Do that in all of your prayer." This will come later. Also among the evidence for this is what Abu Dawud narrated from Nafi' ibn Mahmud ibn al-Rabi' al-Ansari, who said: Ubadah ibn al-Samit was late for the dawn prayer, so Abu Nu'aym the muezzin gave the iqamah, and Abu Nu'aym led the people in prayer. Ubadah ibn al-Samit came, and I was with him, until we lined up behind Abu Nu'aym, and Abu Nu'aym was reciting aloud. Ubadah began to recite Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an, i.e., al-Fatihah). When he finished, I said to Ubadah: "I heard you reciting Umm al-Qur'an while Abu Nu'aym was reciting aloud?" He said: "Indeed! The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in some of the prayers in which the recitation is aloud, and the recitation became confused for him. When he finished, he turned to us with his face and said: 'Do you recite when I recite aloud?' Some of us said: 'We do that.' He said: 'Do not. I say, what is wrong with me that the Qur'an is being disputed by me? Do not recite anything of the Qur'an when I recite aloud except Umm al-Qur'an.'" This is an explicit text regarding the follower (al-ma'mum, the one praying behind the imam). Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi also narrated it from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Ishaq with the same meaning, and said: "It is a good (hasan) hadith." The practice according to this hadith regarding recitation behind the imam is that of most of the people of knowledge among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Successors (al-Tabi'un), and it is the view of Malik ibn Anas, Ibn al-Mubarak, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq, who hold that one recites behind the imam. Al-Daraqutni also narrated it and said: "This chain is good (hasan), and all its narrators are trustworthy (thiqat)." He mentioned that Mahmud ibn al-Rabi' used to reside in Iliya [[Iliya: the name of the city of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis).]], and that Abu Nu'aym was the first to give the adhan in Bayt al-Maqdis. Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq said: Nafi' ibn Mahmud is not mentioned by al-Bukhari in his History, nor by Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bukhari and Muslim did not narrate anything from him. Abu Umar said about him: "Majhul (unknown)." Al-Daraqutni mentioned from Yazid ibn Shurayk, who said: I asked Umar about reciting behind the imam, and he ordered me to recite. I said: "Even if you are the one (leading)?" He said: "Even if I am." I said: "Even if you recite aloud?" He said: "Even if I recite aloud." Al-Daraqutni said: "This chain is sahih (sound)." It is also narrated from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The imam is a guarantor; so whatever he does, do likewise." Abu Hatim said: "This is authentic (yasihhu) for those who hold the view of reciting behind the imam." Abu Hurayrah al-Farisi also issued a ruling according to this, that one should recite silently to oneself, when he was told: "Sometimes I am behind the imam..." Then he cited the saying of the Exalted: [[Meaning in the hadith qudsi.]] "I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves: half of it is for Me, and half of it is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Recite. The servant says: 'Al-hamdu lillahi Rabbi al-'alamin'..." and the hadith continues.

**The Tenth (Point).** As for what the early scholars used as evidence, namely his (upon him be peace) saying: "And when he recites, then be silent," which Muslim narrated from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. He said: In the hadith of Jarir from Sulayman from Qatadah, among the additions is: "And when he recites, then be silent." Al-Daraqutni said: "This wording was not followed by Sulayman al-Taymi in it from Qatadah, and the memorizers (al-huffaz) among the companions of Qatadah opposed him and did not mention it, among them Shu'bah, Hisham, Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah, Hammam, Abu Awanah, Ma'mar, and Adi ibn Abi Umarah." Al-Daraqutni said: "Their consensus indicates his error." It has been narrated from Abd Allah ibn Amir from Qatadah a follow-up (mutabaʿah) for al-Taymi, but he is not strong; al-Qattan abandoned him (taraka). Abu Dawud also narrated this addition from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and said: "This addition, 'And when he recites, then be silent,' is not preserved (mahfuzah)." Abu Muhammad Abd al-Haqq mentioned that Muslim authenticated the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and said: "It is sahih in my view." I say: What indicates its soundness in his view is his inclusion of it in his book from the hadith of Abu Musa, even though it is one of the things on which they did not agree. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Ibn al-Mundhir also authenticated it. As for the saying of the Exalted: "And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent" [al-A'raf: 204], it was revealed in Makkah, while the prohibition of speech in the prayer was revealed in Madinah, as Zayd ibn Arqam said, so there is no proof in it, for its intended audience was the polytheists, according to what Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said. Al-Daraqutni also narrated from Abu Hurayrah that it was revealed concerning raising the voice behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in prayer. He said: "Abd Allah ibn Amir is weak (da'if)." As for his (upon him be peace) saying: "What is wrong with me that the Qur'an is being disputed by me?" Malik narrated it from Ibn Shihab from Ibn Ukaymah al-Laythi, whose name, according to Malik, is Amr; others say Amir, and it was said Yazid, and it was said Umarah, and it was said Abbad. He is known by the kunyah Abu al-Walid. He died in the year 101 AH at the age of seventy-nine. Al-Zuhri narrated from him only this single hadith, and he is trustworthy (thiqah). Muhammad ibn Amr and others narrated from him. The meaning in his hadith is: "Do not raise your voices when I raise mine, for that is dispute, pulling and tugging; recite to yourselves." This is clarified by the hadith of Ubadah, and by the ruling of al-Faruq (Umar) and of Abu Hurayrah, the narrator of both hadiths. For if the prohibition in his saying "What is wrong with me that the Qur'an is being disputed by me?" were understood in its general sense, they would not have issued a ruling contrary to it. And al-Zuhri's statement in the hadith of Ibn Ukaymah: "So the people stopped reciting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited aloud, when they heard that from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," he means by "the Opening" (al-hamd) according to what we have explained. And with Allah is our success. As for his (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever has an imam, the recitation of the imam is his recitation," it is a weak hadith, which al-Hasan ibn Umarah transmitted, and he is abandoned (matruk), and Abu Hanifah [[He is mentioned by Ibn Hajar in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Khallikan in al-Wafayat, and they did not mention any weakness in him regarding hadith, but Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat described him with that.]] and he is weak, both of them from Musa ibn Abi Aishah from Abd Allah ibn Shaddad from Jabir. Al-Daraqutni narrated it and said: "It was narrated by Sufyan al-Thawri, Shu'bah, Israil ibn Yunus, Shurayk, Abu Khalid al-Dalani, Abu al-Ahwas, Sufyan ibn Uyaynah, Jarir ibn Abd al-Hamid and others, from Musa ibn Abi Aishah from Abd Allah ibn Shaddad as a mursal (a hadith in which the Successor attributes it directly to the Prophet, omitting the Companion) from the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is the correct version." As for Jabir's saying: "Whoever prays a rak'ah in which he does not recite Umm al-Qur'an, has not prayed except behind the imam," Malik narrated it from Wahb ibn Kaysan from Jabir as his own statement. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Yahya ibn Sallam, the author of the tafsir, narrated it from Malik from Abu Nu'aym Wahb ibn Kaysan from Jabir from the Prophet (ﷺ), but its correct form is mawquf (halted at Jabir) as in the Muwatta'. In it is a point of jurisprudence: the invalidation of a rak'ah in which Umm al-Qur'an is not recited, and this supports the view of Ibn al-Qasim, who narrated from Malik regarding the nullification of the rak'ah and building upon another, and that the one praying does not count a rak'ah in which he does not recite the Opening of the Book. Also in it: the imam's recitation is a recitation for those behind him. This is the view of Jabir, and others have opposed him in it.

**The Eleventh issue.** Ibn al-Arabi said: When the Prophet ﷺ said, "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book" (Fatihat al-Kitab), people differed over whether this negation is to be taken as referring to completeness and perfection, or to validity (ijza'). Rulings varied according to the differing circumstances of the one examining. Since the more well-known and stronger view on this principle is that the negation is general, the stronger opinion from the narration of Malik is that whoever does not recite the Fatihah in his prayer, his prayer is invalid. Then we considered its repetition in every rak'ah. Whoever interprets the Prophet's ﷺ saying, "Do that in all your prayers," is obliged to repeat the recitation just as he repeats the bowing and prostration. And Allah knows best.

**The Twelfth issue.** What we have mentioned in this chapter, from the hadiths and meanings concerning the specification of the Fatihah, refutes the Kufans' view that the Fatihah is not specified, and that it and other verses of the Qur'an are equal. The Prophet ﷺ specified it by his saying as we have mentioned, and he is the one who explains from Allah, the Exalted, His intended meaning in His saying: "And establish the prayer" (Qur'an 2:43). Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "We were commanded to recite the Opening of the Book and whatever is easy." This hadith indicates that the Prophet's ﷺ saying to the Bedouin, "Recite what is easy for you of the Qur'an," refers to what is beyond the Fatihah, and it is the explanation of Allah's saying: "So recite what is easy of it" (Qur'an 73:20). Muslim narrated from Ubadah ibn al-Samit that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Mother of the Qur'an," and in one narration he added, "and more." His saying ﷺ, "It is deficient (khidaj), three times, incomplete (ghayr tamam)," means not valid according to the mentioned evidences. Khidaj means deficiency and corruption. Al-Akhfash said: "The she-camel miscarried (khadajat) when she delivered her young before completion, and aborted (akhdajat) when she expelled it before the time of birth, even if it was fully formed." Reasoning requires, regarding deficiency, that prayer is not valid with it, because it is a prayer that is not complete, and whoever exits his prayer while it is incomplete must repeat it as he was commanded, according to its ruling. Whoever claims that it is valid while admitting its deficiency must provide the evidence, and there is no way to that which is binding. And Allah knows best.

**The Thirteenth issue.** It is narrated from Malik that recitation is not obligatory in any part of the prayer. Likewise, al-Shafi'i used to say this in Iraq regarding one who forgot it, but then he retracted this in Egypt and said: The prayer of one who knows the Opening of the Book is not valid except with it, and it is not valid for him to omit a single letter of it. If he does not recite it, or omits a letter from it, he must repeat his prayer even if he recited something else. This is the correct view on the question. As for what is narrated from Umar, may Allah have mercy on him, that he prayed the Maghrib and did not recite in it, and it was mentioned to him, and he said: "How were the bowing and prostration?" They said: "Good." He said: "No harm then." This is a hadith with an objectionable wording and a broken chain (munqati' al-isnad), because Ibrahim ibn al-Harith al-Taymi narrates it from Umar, and at other times Ibrahim narrates it from Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman from Umar, and both are broken (munqati'), with no proof in them. Malik mentioned it in the Muwatta', but it is found with some narrators and not with Yahya and a group with him, because Malik removed it from his book later [[i.e., with lateness and distance from good]], and said: "The practice does not follow it, because the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Every prayer in which the Mother of the Qur'an is not recited is deficient (khidaj).'" It is narrated from Umar that he repeated that prayer, and this is the correct report from him. Yahya ibn Yahya al-Nisaburi narrated: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us from al-A'mash from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i from Hammam ibn al-Harith that Umar forgot the recitation in the Maghrib, so he repeated the prayer with them. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: This is a connected hadith, which Hammam witnessed from Umar, and it is narrated through several routes. Ashhab narrated from Malik, who said: Malik was asked about one who forgot the recitation, "Does what Umar said please you?" He said: "I deny that Umar did this," and he rejected the hadith and said: "People would see Umar doing this in the Maghrib and would not glorify Allah with it!" I hold that whoever does this must repeat the prayer.

**The Fourteenth issue:** The scholars agreed that there is no prayer except with recitation, according to what preceded of their principles in this matter. They agreed that there is no specified amount of recitation after the Opening of the Book, except that they recommend not reciting with the Opening of the Book except one surah, because that is the most that came from the Prophet ﷺ. Malik said: The sunnah of recitation is that one recites in the first two rak'ahs the Mother of the Qur'an and a surah, and in the last two the Opening of the Book. Al-Awza'i said: One recites the Mother of the Qur'an. If he does not recite the Mother of the Qur'an and recites something else, it suffices him. He said: If he forgets to recite in three rak'ahs, he must repeat. Al-Thawri said: One recites in the first two rak'ahs the Opening of the Book and a surah, and in the last two he glorifies Allah if he wishes, and if he wishes he recites. If he neither recites nor glorifies, his prayer is valid. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and the rest of the Kufans. Ibn al-Mundhir said: It has been narrated to us from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Recite in the first two and glorify in the last two," and al-Nakha'i said likewise. Sufyan said: If he does not recite in three rak'ahs he must repeat the prayer, because the recitation of one rak'ah does not suffice him. He said: The same applies if he forgets to recite in one rak'ah of the Fajr prayer. Abu Thawr said: No prayer is valid without reciting the Opening of the Book in every rak'ah, like the view of al-Shafi'i of Egypt, and the body of al-Shafi'i's companions hold this, and likewise Ibn Khuwayz Mindad the Maliki said: "Reciting the Fatihah is obligatory for us in every rak'ah, and this is the correct view on the question." Muslim narrated from Abu Qatadah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to lead us in prayer, reciting in Dhuhr and Asr, in the first two rak'ahs, the Opening of the Book and two surahs, and sometimes he would let us hear the verse. He would lengthen the first rak'ah of Dhuhr and shorten the second, and likewise in Subh. In another narration: "And he would recite in the last two rak'ahs the Opening of the Book." This is an explicit text and a sound hadith supporting what Malik held, and an explicit text on the specification of the Fatihah in every rak'ah, against those who refuse this, and the proof is in the Sunnah, not in what opposes it.

**The Fifteenth issue:** The majority held that what is recited beyond the Fatihah is not obligatory, because of what Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "In every prayer there is recitation. What the Prophet ﷺ made us hear, we make you hear; and what he kept hidden from us, we keep hidden from you. Whoever recites the Mother of the Qur'an, it suffices him, and whoever adds, it is better." In al-Bukhari: "And if you add, it is better." Many scholars refused to omit the surah, whether out of necessity or not, among them Imran ibn Husayn, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Khawwat ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Abu Wa'il, Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, and others. They said: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite in it the Opening of the Book and something else from the Qur'an with it." Some of them specified two verses, some specified one verse, and some did not specify, saying: "Something of the Qur'an with it." All of this requires learning what is easy of the Qur'an in every case along with the Opening of the Book, based on the hadith of Ubadah, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and others. In the Mudawwana: Waki' from al-A'mash from Khaythamah said: "Someone told me that he heard Umar ibn al-Khattab say: 'The prayer of one who does not recite in it the Opening of the Book and something with it is not valid.'" The school differed concerning the recitation of a surah on three views: sunnah, virtuous (fadilah), and obligatory.

**The Sixteenth issue:** If it is impossible for someone, after exerting his utmost effort, to learn the Fatihah or any part of the Qur'an, and nothing of it has stuck to him, he must mention Allah in the place of recitation with whatever he can of takbir, tahlil, tahmid, tasbih, tamjid, or "There is no power nor strength except with Allah," when praying alone or with an imam in what the imam recites silently. Abu Dawud and others narrated from Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, who said: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "I cannot take anything from the Qur'an, so teach me what suffices me of it." He said: "Say: Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and there is no power nor strength except with Allah." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is for Allah, so what is for me?" He said: "Say: O Allah, have mercy on me, grant me well-being, guide me, and provide for me."

**The Seventeenth issue:** If he is unable to get any of this wording right, he should not abandon the prayer with the imam to the best of his ability, and the imam will bear that for him, God willing. He must always strive to learn the Fatihah and beyond, until death comes between him and that while he is still striving, and Allah will excuse him.

**The Eighteenth issue:** Whoever's tongue does not manage to speak Arabic, from among non-Arabs and others, the Arabic supplication is to be translated for him into the language he understands in order to establish his prayer, for that suffices him, God willing, Exalted is He.

**The Nineteenth issue:** The prayer of one who recites in Persian while he is able to speak Arabic is not valid according to the majority. Abu Hanifa said: Recitation in Persian suffices him even if he is able to speak Arabic, because the aim is to hit the meaning. Ibn al-Mundhir said: That does not suffice him, because it contradicts what Allah commanded, and contradicts what the Prophet ﷺ taught, and contradicts the communities of Muslims. We do not know of anyone who agreed with him on what he said.

**The Twentieth issue:** Whoever begins the prayer as commanded while not knowing the recitation, and knowledge of it comes to him during the prayer, and this can be imagined by his having heard someone recite it so that it stuck in his memory from mere hearing, he does not restart the prayer, because he has performed what preceded according to what he was commanded, so there is no reason to invalidate it. This is said in the Book of Ibn Sahnun.

**Chapter Three: On saying "Amin," and it contains eight issues.**

**The first issue:** It is recommended for the reciter of the Qur'an, after finishing al-Fatihah and after a brief pause on the *nun* of "﴿nor of those who are astray﴾," to say *amin* (meaning "So be it"), so that what is Qur'an is distinguished from what is not Qur'an.

**The second issue:** It is established in the authoritative collections, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the imam says *amin*, then say *amin*, for whoever's *amin* coincides with the *amin* of the angels, his past sins will be forgiven." Our scholars (may Allah have mercy on them) said: The forgiveness of sin is connected to four preliminaries contained in this hadith. The first: the imam's saying *amin*. The second: the saying of *amin* by those behind him. The third: the saying of *amin* by the angels. The fourth: the coincidence of the *amin*. It has been said that this refers to the response (being answered), and it has been said that it refers to the time, and it has been said that it refers to the manner, namely the sincerity of the supplication, due to his (ﷺ) saying: "Call upon Allah while you are certain of being answered, and know that Allah does not respond to a supplication from a heart that is heedless and distracted."

**The third issue:** Abu Dawud related from Abu Musabbih al-Muqra'i, who said: "We used to sit with Abu Zuhayr al-Numayri, who was one of the Companions, and he would narrate the best of narrations. When one of us made a supplication, he would say: 'Seal it with *amin*, for *amin* is like the seal upon the scroll.'" Abu Zuhayr said: "Shall I not inform you about that? We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) one night, and we came upon a man who had been insistent in his request. The Prophet (ﷺ) stopped to listen to him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'He has made it obligatory, if he seals it.'" A man from the people said to him: "With what should he seal it?" He said: "With *amin*, for whoever seals with *amin* has made it obligatory." The man who had asked the Prophet (ﷺ) departed, came to the man and said to him: "Seal it, O so-and-so, and rejoice."

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Abu Zuhayr al-Numayri, his name is Yahya ibn Nufayr. He related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not kill locusts, for they are the greatest army of Allah."

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "*Amin* is four letters. Allah creates from each letter an angel who says: 'O Allah, forgive whoever says *amin*.'"

In a report: "Jibril taught me *amin* at the end of my recitation of the Opening of the Book, and he said: 'It is like the seal upon the book.'" In another hadith: "*Amin* is the seal of the Lord of the worlds."

Al-Harawi said: Abu Bakr said: Its meaning is that it is the seal of Allah upon His servants, because by it He repels calamities and afflictions from them. So it is like the seal of the book, which protects it and prevents its corruption and the disclosure of what is within it.

In another hadith: "*Amin* is a degree in Paradise." Abu Bakr said: Its meaning is that it is a letter by which the one who says it acquires a degree in Paradise.

**The fourth issue:** The meaning of *amin*, according to most of the people of knowledge, is: "O Allah, respond to us," placed in the position of supplication. Some people said: It is one of the names of Allah. This was related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Mujahid, and Hilal ibn Yasaf, and Ibn Abbas related it from the Prophet (ﷺ), but it is not authentic; this was stated by Ibn al-Arabi. It has been said that the meaning of *amin* is: "So let it be," as stated by al-Jawhari.

al-Kalbi related from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): What is the meaning of *amin*?" He said: "My Lord, do it." Muqatil said: It is a strengthening of the supplication and a drawing down of blessing. al-Tirmidhi said: Its meaning is: "Do not disappoint our hope."

**The fifth issue:** There are two dialects for *amin*: the lengthened form, on the pattern of *fa'il* like *Yasin*, and the shortened form, on the pattern of *yamin*. The poet said, using the lengthened form:

*"O Lord, do not deprive me of her love ever,
And may Allah have mercy on a servant who says 'amin.'"*

Another said:

*"Amin, amin, I will not be satisfied with one,
Until I reach with it two thousand amins."*

Another said, using the shortened form:

*"A great man distanced himself from me when I asked him
For amin, so Allah increased the distance between us."*

Shaddah on the *mim* is an error, said al-Jawhari. However, it has been related from al-Hasan and Ja'far al-Sadiq with shaddah, and this is the view of al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl, from *amma*, meaning "he intended," that is, "we are intending toward You." From this is His saying: ﴿Nor those heading to the Sacred House﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. This was related by Abu Nasr Abd al-Rahim ibn Abd al-Karim al-Qushayri. Al-Jawhari said: It is built on fatha, like *ayna* and *kayfa*, because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. You say from it: "So-and-so said *amin*, a saying of *amin* (ta'min)."

**The sixth issue:** The scholars differed over whether the imam says it and whether he says it aloud. Al-Shafi'i and Malik, in a narration from the people of Madinah, held that he does. The Kufans and some of the people of Madinah said: He does not say it aloud. This is the view of al-Tabari, and Ibn Habib of our scholars also said so. Ibn Bukayr said: It is optional. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik that the imam does not say *amin*; rather, only those behind him say it. This is the view of Ibn al-Qasim and the Egyptian companions of Malik. Their proof is the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us, explained our sunnah to us, and taught us our prayer, and he said: "When you pray, straighten your rows, then let one of you lead you. When he says *takbir*, then say *takbir*, and when he says ﴿not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾, then say *amin*, and Allah will respond to you." He mentioned the hadith, which Muslim recorded. Similar is the hadith of Sumayy from Abu Hurayrah, which Malik recorded.

The correct view is the first, based on the hadith of Wa'il ibn Hujr who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾, he said: '*Amin*,' raising his voice with it." Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni recorded it, and al-Daraqutni added: "Abu Bakr said: This is a sunnah in which the people of Kufah alone were unique; this (hadith) is authentic, and what follows it (is also)." Al-Bukhari titled a chapter: "The chapter on the imam's loud saying of *amin*." Ata said: "*Amin* is a supplication. Ibn al-Zubayr and those behind him said *amin*, until the mosque resonated with a roar." (*al-lujjah* means the sound.)

al-Tirmidhi said: Many of the people of knowledge from among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and those after them held this view, that a man should raise his voice with *amin* and not conceal it. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq. In the Muwatta' and the Sahihayn, Ibn Shihab said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: *amin*." In Sunan Ibn Majah, from Abu Hurayrah, he said: "The people abandoned *amin*, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he said ﴿not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray﴾, would say *amin*, until the people of the first row could hear it, and the mosque would shake with it."

As for the hadith of Abu Musa and Sumayy, their meaning is to define the place at which *amin* is said, which is when the imam says ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾, so that their saying is simultaneous, and they do not precede him with the saying of *amin*, for the reason we have mentioned. And Allah knows best. This is also due to his (ﷺ) saying: "When the imam says *amin*, then say *amin*."

Ibn Nafi' said in the book of Ibn al-Harith: The follower should not say it unless he hears the imam saying ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾. If he is at a distance where he cannot hear him, he should not say it. Ibn Abdus said: He should estimate the length of the recitation and then say *amin*.

**The seventh issue:** The companions of Abu Hanifah said: Silent *amin* is better than saying it aloud, because it is a supplication, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾ [al-A'raf: 55]. They said: The evidence for this is what is reported concerning the interpretation of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Your supplication has been answered, both of you﴾ [Yunus: 89]. He said: Musa was supplicating and Harun was saying *amin*, so Allah called them both supplicants.

The answer: The concealment of supplication is only better because of the element of showing off (riya') that may enter into it. As for what relates to congregational prayer, attending it is the public display of an outward symbol and the manifestation of a truth to which the servants are encouraged to give expression. The imam has been encouraged to publicize the recitation of al-Fatihah, which includes supplication, and its closing *amin*. So when the supplication is one for which loud recitation is recommended, then saying *amin* over the supplication follows it and takes its place. This is clear.

**The eighth issue:** The word *amin* was not known before us except for Musa and Harun (peace be upon them). al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim mentioned in *Nawadir al-Usul*: Abd al-Warith ibn Abd al-Samad narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, saying: Razin, the muezzin of the mosque of Hisham ibn Hassan, narrated to us, saying: Anas ibn Malik narrated to us, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has given my nation three things that He has given to no one before them: the greeting of peace, which is the greeting of the people of Paradise; the ranks of the angels; and *amin*, except what was given to Musa and Harun." Abu Abd Allah said: Its meaning is that Musa supplicated against Pharaoh, and Harun said *amin*. So when Allah, blessed is His name, mentioned the supplication of Musa in His revelation, He said: ﴿Your supplication has been answered, both of you﴾ [Yunus: 89], and He did not mention the statement of Harun. Musa said: "Our Lord," so from Harun was the *amin*, and He called him a supplicant in His revelation, since He made that from him a supplication.

It has been said that *amin* is specific to this nation, due to what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The Jews have never envied you for anything as they have envied you for the greeting of peace and for *amin*." Ibn Majah recorded it through the narration of Hammad ibn Salamah, from Suhayl ibn Abi Salih, from his father, from Aisha, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said... the hadith. He also recorded, from the narration of Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Jews have never envied you for anything as they have envied you for *amin*, so increase your saying of *amin*."

Our scholars (may Allah have mercy on them) said: [This is an interpretation by them of the hadith as applying to al-Fatihah together with *amin* at its end.] The People of the Book envied us because its beginning is praise of Allah and His commendation, then humility before Him and submission, then a supplication for us for guidance to the straight path, then the supplication against them together with our saying *amin*.

**Chapter Four:** On what al-Fatihah contains of meanings, recitations, grammatical analysis, and the virtue of those who praise (Allah). It contains thirty-six issues.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 1, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

The first issue: His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾. Abu Muhammad Abd al-Ghani ibn Sa'id al-Hafiz related, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "When the servant says, 'All praise is due to Allah,' Allah says, 'My servant has spoken truly; the praise is Mine.'" Muslim related from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah is pleased with the servant who eats a morsel and praises Him for it, or drinks a drink and praises Him for it." Al-Hasan said: "No blessing exists except that the praise of Allah is better than it." Ibn Majah related from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whenever Allah bestows a blessing upon a servant and he says, 'All praise is due to Allah,' what he has been given is better than what he has taken." In Nawadir al-Usul, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If the whole world, in its entirety, were in the hand of a man of my community, and then he said, 'All praise is due to Allah,' the words 'All praise is due to Allah' would be better than that." Abu Abd Allah said: Its meaning, in our view, is that he has been given the world, and then, immediately after it, he is given this word so that he utters it; thus this word is better than the whole world, because the world is perishing and the word is enduring. It is among "the enduring good deeds," as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the enduring good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord for reward and better for hope﴾ [Maryam: 76]. It was also said in some narrations: "What he gave would be more than what he took." So he made the word a giving from the servant, and the world a taking from Allah. This is in terms of arrangement [in some copies of the original: "in terms of reminder"]. Likewise it applies in speech: this word is from the servant, and the world is from Allah, and both are from Allah in origin: the world is from Him and the word is from Him. He gave him the world and enriched him, and He gave him the word and ennobled him by it in the Hereafter. Ibn Majah related from Ibn Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told them: "A servant of Allah's servants said, 'O Lord, to You is praise as befits the majesty of Your Face and the greatness of Your sovereignty.' The two angels were confounded and did not know how to record it. They ascended to heaven and said, 'Our Lord, Your servant has uttered a saying we do not know how to record.' Allah, Mighty and Majestic, who knows best what His servant said, said, 'What did My servant say?' They said, 'O Lord, he said: "O Lord, to You is praise as befits the majesty of Your Face and the greatness of Your sovereignty."' Allah said to them, 'Record it as My servant said, until he meets Me, and I will reward him for it.'" The lexicographers said: a'dala al-amr means it became severe and difficult to resolve, and al-mu'addalat (with the ḍad doubled) are difficulties. 'Adalat al-mar'ah wa al-shah means when the offspring of a woman or a ewe is stuck and its exit is not easy, also with the ḍad doubled. Accordingly, it would be: a'dalat al-malakayn, or 'addalat al-mulkayn without the bā'. And Allah knows best. It is related from Muslim, from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Purity is half of faith, and 'All praise is due to Allah' fills the scale, and 'Glory be to Allah' and 'All praise is due to Allah' fill—or fill what is between the heavens and the earth." And he mentioned the hadith.

The second issue: The scholars differed over which is more excellent: the servant's saying "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds," or the saying "There is no god but Allah"? One group said: his saying "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds" is more excellent, because it includes within it the tawhid which is "There is no god but Allah." So in his saying there is both tawhid and praise, whereas in "There is no god but Allah" there is only tawhid. Another group said: "There is no god but Allah" is more excellent, because it repels disbelief and polytheism, and upon it creation is fought. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say, 'There is no god but Allah.'" Ibn Atiyyah chose this view, and he said: The criterion for this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best thing I and the prophets before me have said is: There is no god but Allah, alone, without partner."

The third issue: The Muslims have agreed that Allah is praised for all His blessings, and that among the blessings Allah has bestowed is faith. This indicates that faith is His act and His creation. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. "The worlds" is the totality of created beings, and faith is among them, contrary to what the Qadariyyah said: that it is a creation of theirs, as its explanation will come.

The fourth issue: In the speech of the Arabs, al-hamd means complete praise, and the definite article [alif and lam] is for the comprehensiveness of the category of praiseworthy qualities. Thus He, glorified is He, deserves all praise in its entirety, since He possesses the Most Beautiful Names and the Highest Attributes. The word hamd has been put in the plural of paucity in the saying of the poet:
"A radiant one, praised in his commendation, I have singled him out with the best of my words and the best of my praises."
So hamd is the opposite of dhamm (blame). You say: hamidtu al-rajul ahmaduhu hamdan, fa-huwa hamid wa mahmud, and al-tahmid is more emphatic than al-hamd. Al-hamd is more general than al-shukr. And al-muhammad is one in whom the praiseworthy qualities are abundant. The poet said:
"To the noble, generous, lordly, much-praised one."
By this the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was named. And the poet said: [He is Hassan ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him.]
"He derived for him from His name so as to exalt him: the Lord of the Throne is Mahmud, and this is Muhammad."
Al-mahmadah is the opposite of al-madhammah. Ahmada al-rajul means his affair came to praise. Ahmadtuhu means I found him praiseworthy: you say, "I came to such-and-such a place and found it agreeable (fa-ahmadtuhu)," meaning I found it praiseworthy and suitable, and that is when you are pleased with its dwelling or pasture. A man who is hamadah, on the pattern of humazah, praises things excessively and says of them more than what is in them. And hamadat al-nar, with a vowel on the middle letter, is the sound of its blazing.

The fifth issue: Abu Ja'far al-Tabari and Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad held that hamd and shukr have one and the same meaning, but this is not an acceptable view. Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami related it in his book "al-Haqa'iq" from Ja'far al-Sadiq and Ibn Ata'. Ibn Ata' said: its meaning is thanks to Allah, since from Him comes the bestowal of teaching us Him, until we praised Him. Al-Tabari argued that they have the same meaning from the soundness of your saying: "al-hamdu lillah shukran" (All praise is due to Allah, as thanks). Ibn Atiyyah said: In reality this is evidence against what he held, because when you say "shukran," you have specified praise for it because it is for a blessing among blessings. Some scholars said: shukr is more general than hamd, because it is by the tongue, by the limbs, and by the heart, whereas hamd is only by the tongue. It was also said: hamd is more general, because it contains the meaning of thanks and the meaning of praise, and it is more general than thanks, because hamd is placed where thanks is placed, but thanks is not placed where hamd is placed. It is related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "All praise is due to Allah" is the word of every thankful person, and that Adam, upon him be peace, said when he sneezed: "All praise is due to Allah." And Allah said to Noah, upon him be peace: ﴿Say: All praise is due to Allah, who has saved us from the wrongdoing people﴾ [[Verse 28, Surah al-Mu'minun.]]. Ibrahim, upon him be peace, said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has granted me in old age Isma'il and Ishaq﴾ [[Verse 39, Surah Ibrahim.]]. In the story of Dawud and Sulayman He said: ﴿And they both said: All praise is due to Allah, who has favored us over many of His believing servants﴾ [[Verse 15, Surah al-Naml.]]. He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And say: All praise is due to Allah, who has not taken a son﴾ [[Verse 111, Surah al-Isra'.]]. The people of Paradise said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has removed from us grief﴾ [[Verse 34, Surah Fatir.]]. ﴿And the last of their call is: All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [[Verse 10, Surah Yunus.]]. Thus it is the word of every thankful person. I say: The correct view is that hamd is praise of the one praised for his attributes without any prior benefaction, while shukr is praise of the one thanked for the benefaction he has conferred. [Ibn Atiyyah, in his commentary, followed this by saying: The praiser among people is of two kinds: the thankful one and the one who praises by attributes. With this the author's words are clarified.] On this definition our scholars said: hamd is more general than shukr, because hamd applies to praise, to glorification, and to thanks, whereas recompense is specific, given only as a reward to one who has conferred a kindness upon you. So hamd becomes more general in the verse, because it exceeds shukr. Hamd is also used in the sense of contentment: it is said, "I tested him and so I praised him," meaning I was content with him. From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿a praiseworthy station﴾ [[Verse 79, Surah al-Isra'.]]. And he, upon him be peace, said: "I am content with you in cleansing the urethra" (ahmadu ilaykum ghasl al-ihlil), meaning I am pleased with it for you. It is related from Ja'far al-Sadiq concerning His saying "All praise is due to Allah": whoever praises Him by His attributes as He described Himself has praised Him, for hamd comes with ha', mim and dal: the ha' is from wahdaniyyah (oneness), the mim is from al-mulk (sovereignty), and the dal is from al-daymumiyyah (perpetuity). Whoever knows Him by oneness, perpetuity and sovereignty has known Him, and this is the reality of "All praise is due to Allah." Shaqiq ibn Ibrahim said, in explaining "All praise is due to Allah": it has three aspects. The first: when Allah gives you something, you recognize who gave it to you. The second: that you are content with what He has given you. The third: that as long as His strength is in your body, you do not disobey Him. These are the conditions of praise.

The sixth issue: Allah, glorified is He, praised Himself, and opened His Book with His praise, and He did not permit this to anyone else. Rather, He forbade them from it in His Book and on the tongue of His Prophet, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿So do not attest to your own purity; He knows best who is pious﴾ [[Verse 32, Surah al-Najm.]]. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Throw dust in the faces of the praisers" [narrated by al-Miqdad]. The discussion of this will come in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 246]], if Allah the Exalted wills. So the meaning of "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds" is: praise has preceded from Me for Myself, before anyone among the worlds could praise Me; and My praise of Myself for Myself in eternity was without any cause, whereas my praise of creation is mixed with causes. Our scholars said: it is disgraceful for a creature who has not been given perfection to praise himself in order to draw benefits to himself and repel harms from himself. It was also said: when He, glorified is He, knew the incapacity of His servants to praise Him, He praised Himself by Himself, for Himself, in eternity; thus the exhaustion of His servants' strength is the very place of their incapacity to praise Him. Do you not see that the master of the messengers displayed incapacity when he said: "I cannot enumerate praise of You"? And they recited:
"When we praise You with what is good, You are as we praise, and above what we praise."

It has been said: He praised Himself in eternity, because He knew of the abundance of His blessings upon His servants and their inability to fulfill the obligation of praising Him; so He praised Himself on their behalf, so that the blessing would be more wholesome for them, since by this He removed from them the burden of obligation.

The seventh issue: The seven readers (al-Qurra' al-Sab'a) and the majority of people agreed on raising the dal in "al-hamdu lillah." It is narrated from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna and Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj that they read "al-hamda lillah" with the dal in the accusative case, and this is by way of an implied verb (fa'ala). It is also said: "al-hamdu lillah" with the raised case, as a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). The nature of a predicate is that it conveys information, so what is the benefit here? The answer: Sibawayh said: When a man says "al-hamdu lillah" in the nominative, it carries the same meaning as your saying "hamistu Allaha hamdan" (I praised Allah with praise), except that whoever uses the nominative for al-hamd informs that the praise comes from Him and from all creation to Allah, while whoever uses the accusative for al-hamd informs that the praise comes from Him alone to Allah. Others besides Sibawayh said: This is only said as an approach to Allah's pardon and forgiveness, and as glorification and exaltation of Him; it departs from the meaning of a predicate and carries the meaning of a request. It is in a hadith: "Whoever is occupied with remembering Me instead of asking Me, I will give him the best of what I give to those who ask." It is also said: His praising Himself and His commending Himself is to teach that to His servants, so the meaning according to this is: Say, "al-hamdu lillah." Al-Tabari said: "al-hamdu lillah" is a praise by which He praised Himself, and implicitly He commanded His servants to praise Him; it is as if He said: Say, "al-hamdu lillah." On this basis, the phrase "qulu iyyaka" (say, "You alone we worship") comes in the same way. This is one of the Arabs' omissions, where the apparent sense of the speech points to what is omitted, as the poet said:

"And I know that I will become a grave-mound
when the swift camels (al-nawaji: swift ones of the camels) pass without stopping"

"The questioners asked: For whom did you dig?
The answerers said: For him, a vizier."

The meaning: The one dug for is a vizier. It was omitted because the apparent sense of the speech points to it, and this is common. It is narrated from Ibn Abi 'Abla: "al-hamdu lillah" with a dammah on the dal and the lam, to make the second follow the first and to harmonize the wording. Seeking harmony in pronunciation is common in their speech, as in "ajuwuka" and "huwa munhadarun min al-jabal," with dammah on the dal and the jim. He said:

"Strike the two shins; your mother is bereaved (habil)"

with a dammah on the nun, due to the dammah on the hamzah. In a reading of the people of Makkah, "murdifin" with a dammah on the ra' to follow the mim, and likewise "muquttilin" with a dammah on the qaf. They also said "li-immika," breaking the hamzah to follow the lam. And there was recited for al-Nu'man ibn Bashir:

"Woe to its mother, in the air of the sky, pursuing,
and there is none like this on the earth that is sought."

(It describes an eagle pursuing a wolf to hunt it. Sibawayh attributed this line once to al-Nu'man (vol. 2, p. 272) and another time to Imru' al-Qays (vol. 1, p. 353). Al-Baghdadi in Khizanat al-Adab, shahid 266, also attributes it to Imru' al-Qays, and it appears in his diwan as: "la kalladhi fi hawa' al-jaww...", and on this basis there is no evidence in it.)

The original is: "wayl li-ummiha," so the first lam was deleted, and the dammah on the hamzah after a kasrah was felt to be heavy, so it was moved to the lam, then the lam was made to follow the mim. It is narrated from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Zayd ibn 'Ali: "al-hamdi lillah" with a kasrah on the dal, to make the first follow the second.

The eighth issue: His saying, exalted is He: "Lord of the worlds" (rabbi al-'alamin) (2), that is, their Owner. Whoever possesses something is its lord, so "rabb" means "owner." In al-Sihah: "Rabb" is one of the names of Allah the Exalted, and is not said of anyone else except with an added term (idafa). They used it in the pre-Islamic period for a king. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"He is the Lord and the Witness over the day of
al-Hayarin (a place where the people of al-Mundhir ibn Ma' al-Sama' raided) and the affliction is an affliction."

"Rabb" also means "master," and from it is His saying, exalted is He: "Mention me before your lord" (Yusuf 42). In a hadith: "that a slave-girl gives birth to her mistress (rabbatahā)," that is, her master; and we have explained this in the book al-Tadhkira. "Rabb" also means the reformer, the manager, the one who mends, and the one who sustains. Al-Harawi and others said: It is said of one who undertakes the reform and completion of something: "qad rabbahu yarubbuhu," so he is "rabb" to it and "rabb" (rabbani) — and from this the rabbaniyyun are named, for their upholding of the Books. In a hadith: "Do you have a blessing you maintain upon him?" (hal laka min ni'matin turubbuhā 'alayhi), that is, you attend to it and reform it. "Rabb" also means the worshipped one, and from it is the poet's saying:

"A lord whom the foxes urinate upon at his head?
Indeed he is humiliated, the one upon whom foxes urinate."

It is said in an intensive form (ʿala al-takthir; in al-Nahhas: "al-takbir"): rabbahu, rabbabahu, and rabbatahu, related by al-Nahhas. In al-Sihah: "Fulan raabba his child, yarubbuhu, rabban, and rabbabahu and tarabbabahu" with the same meaning, that is, he raised him. "al-marbub" means the one raised.

The ninth issue: Some scholars said: This name is the Greatest Name of Allah, because of the frequency with which supplicants call upon Him by it. Reflect on this in the Qur'an, as at the end of Al 'Imran (see vol. 4, p. 313) and Surat Ibrahim (see vol. 9, p. 368) and others; and because of what this description implies of the bond between the Lord and the one nurtured, together with what it includes of tenderness, mercy, and need in every state. Its derivation has been disputed. It is said: It is derived from "tarbiya" (upbringing), so Allah, glorified and exalted, is the manager of His creation and their Nurturer; from this is His saying, exalted is He: "And your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship" (al-Nisa' 23). Thus the daughter of a wife is called "rabiba" for the husband's upbringing of her. So, if He is the manager and nurturer of His creation, it is an attribute of action (sifat fi'l); and if "rabb" means owner and master, it is an attribute of essence (sifat dhat).

The tenth issue: When the article "al" is attached to "rabb," it becomes specific to Allah, the Exalted, because it is for definiteness (al-'ahd). If we remove it, it becomes shared between Allah and His servants; one says: "Allah is the lord of the servants," and "Zayd is the lord of the house." So Allah, glorified is He, is "Rabb al-Arbab," who owns the owner and the owned, and He is the creator of that and its provider. Every other lord is neither creator nor provider; every owned thing is owned after not having been, and is dispossessed from one's hand; one owns only some things and not others. The attribute of Allah, the Exalted, differs from these meanings. This is the difference between the attribute of the Creator and that of the created.

The eleventh issue: His saying, exalted is He, "al-'alamin." The interpreters differed greatly over "al-'alamin." Qatadah said: "al-'alamun" is the plural of "'alam," which is every existent other than Allah, the Exalted, and it has no singular from its own form, like "rahṭ" and "qawm." It is also said: The people of each age are an "'alam," said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl, based on His saying, exalted is He: "Do you approach the males of the worlds?" (al-Shu'ara' 165), that is, of the people. Al-'Ajjaj said:

"So Khindif is the head of this 'alam"

(Khindif is the name of an Arab tribe; al-'Allama al-Shanqiti noted that al-'Ajjaj used to recite "al-'alam" with a hamzah and sukun.)

Jarir ibn al-Khatafa said:

"The creation divides it while it is elevated,
and the worlds become dependents to him."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-'alamun" are the jinn and mankind; his evidence is His saying, exalted is He: "That he may be a warner to the worlds" (al-Furqan 1), and he was not a warner to the beasts. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda said: "'alam" refers to those who have intellect, and they are four nations: mankind, the jinn, the angels, and the devils. "'Alam" is not said of beasts, because this plural is specifically the plural of those who have intellect. Al-A'sha said:

"I have not heard of their like among the worlds."

Zayd ibn Aslam said: They are the provision-receivers (al-murtaziqun), and similar is the saying of Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': They are the spiritual beings (al-ruhaniyyun). This is also the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's statement: every living creature that crawls upon the face of the earth. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has eighteen thousand worlds, of which this world is one. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: Allah has forty thousand worlds, and this world from its east to its west is one world. Muqatil said: The worlds are eighty thousand worlds: forty thousand worlds on land and forty thousand worlds in the sea. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas related from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: The jinn are one world, and mankind is one world, and beyond that, for the earth there are four corners, in each corner a thousand and five hundred worlds, which He created to worship Him.

I say: The first opinion is the most correct of these sayings, because it encompasses every created and existing thing, based on His saying, exalted is He: "Pharaoh said: And what is the Lord of the worlds? (Musa) said: Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them" (al-Shu'ara' 23). Then it is derived from "'ilm" (knowledge) and "'alama" (sign), because it indicates its Originator. Thus said al-Zajjaj: The world is everything that Allah created in this world and the Hereafter. Al-Khalil said: "'ilm," "'alama," and "ma'lam" are what indicates a thing, so the world indicates that it has a Creator and Manager, and this is clear.

It is related that a man said in the presence of al-Junayd: "al-hamdu lillah." He said to him: Complete it as Allah said: "Rabb al-'alamin." The man said: And who are the worlds, that they should be mentioned alongside the Truth? He said: Say it, my brother, for when the originated is joined with the Eternal, it leaves no trace.

The twelfth issue: "Rabb" may be read in the nominative or the accusative. The accusative is by way of praise, and the nominative is by way of a new sentence (qat'), meaning: He is the Lord of the worlds.

The thirteenth issue: His saying, "The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful" (3). After "Lord of the worlds," He described Himself as "the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful," because His being "Lord of the worlds" contains an element of intimidation (tarhib), so He joined it with "the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful," since it includes encouragement (targhib). This is so that His attributes combine both awe of Him (al-rahbah minhu) and desire for Him (al-raghbah ilayhi), and so that it is more helpful toward obedience to Him and more effective in restraining from disobedience. As He said: "Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful. And that My punishment is the painful punishment" [Al-Hijr 15:49-50]. And He said: "Forgiver of sin, Acceptor of repentance, Severe in punishment, Possessor of bounty" [Ghafir 40:3].

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If the believer knew what there is with Allah of punishment, none would hope for His Paradise; and if the disbelievers knew what there is with Allah of mercy, none would despair of His Paradise."

The meanings of these two names have already been discussed earlier, so there is no point in repeating them.

The fourteenth point concerns His words, "Master of the Day of Judgment" (4). Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' recited *Maliki* with a fatha on the *mim*. There are four dialectal forms (lughat): *Maaliku*, *Maliku*, *Malku* (a lightened form of *Maliku*), and *Maleeku*. A poet said: [[This is Amr ibn Kulthum.]]

"And days of ours, bright and long, when we disobeyed the king in them by refusing to submit."

Another said: [[This is Labid ibn Rabi'a al-Amiri.]]

"So be content with what the King has apportioned, for it is He who has apportioned creation among us, its Knower."

*Al-khala'iq* means the natural dispositions upon which a person is created. It is reported from Nafi' that he gave the kasra in *Maliki* its full vowel, so that he read *Malikee*, in accordance with the dialect of those who lengthen the vowels. This is an Arabic dialect, as mentioned by al-Mahdawi and others.

The fifteenth point: the scholars differed over which is more eloquent, *Malik* or *Maalik*. Both readings are transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and Umar. al-Tirmidhi mentioned both. It is said that *Maliki* is more general and more eloquent than *Maliki*, since every king is an owner, but not every owner is a king, and because the command of the king takes effect over the owner in his property, so that he does not dispose of anything except under the king's direction. This was said by Abu Ubayda and al-Mubarrad. It is also said that *Maaliki* is more eloquent, because He is the owner of people and others besides them; so the owner has a more powerful and greater authority, since the enforcement of the laws of the Shari'a rests with him, and in addition he has the sense of possession. Abu Ali said: Abu Bakr ibn al-Sarraj related from some of those who preferred the reading *Malik* that God, glorified is He, has described Himself as the owner of everything by His words "Lord of the worlds," so there is no benefit in the reading of those who read *Maaliki*, because it is a repetition. Abu Ali said: There is no proof in this, because in the revelation there are things of this form, in which the general comes first and then the specific is mentioned, such as His words: "He is God, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner" (59:24). *Al-Khaliq* is general, and *al-Musawwir* is mentioned because it draws attention to the craftsmanship and the existence of wisdom. Likewise He said: "And in the Hereafter they are certain" (2:4), after His words "who believe in the unseen." The unseen is general and includes the Hereafter and other things, but the Hereafter is singled out for its greatness, to draw attention to the obligation of believing in it, and to refute the disbelievers who deny it. Likewise He said: "the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful" (1:3). He mentioned *al-Rahman*, which is general, and then *al-Rahim* after it, to single out the believers for it in His words: "And He is ever merciful to the believers" (33:43). Abu Hatim said: *Maalik* is more eloquent than *Malik* in praising the Creator, while *Malik* is more eloquent than *Maalik* in praising created beings. The difference between them is that an owner among created beings may not be a king, whereas if God, exalted is He, is an owner, He is a king. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi chose this view and mentioned three aspects. The first: you attach it to what is specific and to what is general, so you say "owner of the house, the land, the garment," just as you say "owner of the kings." The second: it applies to the owner of a little and of a lot. When you reflect on these two views, you find them to be one. The third: you say "owner of the kingdom" (*malik al-mulk*), and you do not say "king of the kingdom" (*malik al-mulk*). Ibn al-Hassar said: That is because what is meant by *maalik* is indicating ownership with a kasra on the *mim*, and this does not include *al-mulk* with a damma on the *mim*. *Malik*, however, includes both matters together, so it is more emphatic. It also includes perfection, and for this reason one deserves kingship over those below him. Do you not see His words: "God has chosen him over you and increased him abundantly in knowledge and physique" (2:247)? For this reason he (ﷺ) said: "Leadership belongs to Quraysh." Quraysh is the best of the Arab tribes, and the Arabs are better and more honourable than non-Arabs. It also includes power and choice, which is a necessity in a king. If he were not capable, free to choose, with his judgment and command effective, his enemy would overcome him, others would prevail over him, and his subjects would despise him. It also includes seizing, commanding, forbidding, promising and threatening. Do you not see the words of Solomon (peace be upon him): "Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent? I will surely punish him with a severe punishment" (27:20–21)? And other wondrous matters and noble meanings which are not found in *maalik*. I say: Some have argued that *maalik* is more eloquent because it has an extra letter, so the reader of it receives ten good deeds more than the reader of *malik*. I say: This considers the form and not the meaning, and the reading *malik* is established, and it contains meaning which is not in *maalik*, as we have explained. And God knows best.

The sixteenth point: it is not permissible for anyone to be named with this name, nor to be called by it, except God, exalted is He. al-Bukhari and Muslim related from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection God will seize the earth and fold the heavens in His right hand, then He will say: I am the King; where are the kings of the earth?" And also from him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The most despicable name in the sight of God is a man who names himself *malik al-amlak*." Muslim added: "There is no owner but God, Mighty and Majestic." Sufyan said: [[Sufyan here is one of the narrators in this chain.]] "Like *shahan shah*." Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: I asked Abu Amr al-Shaybani about *akhna'*, and he said: "lowest." And from him, he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The man most hateful to God on the Day of Resurrection and the most wicked is a man who was called *malik al-amlak*; there is no king but God, glorified is He." Ibn al-Hassar said: Likewise, "Master of the Day of Judgment" and "Owner of the kingdom" — there should be no disagreement that this is forbidden for all created beings, just as naming someone *malik al-amlak* is forbidden.

As for describing someone with *malik* and *maalik*, the seventeenth point: it is permissible for those who possess their meanings to be described by them. God the Mighty said: "Indeed God has sent Talut to you as king" (2:247). He (ﷺ) said: "Some people of my nation will be shown to me as warriors in the cause of God, riding the middle [*thabaj*: the middle and main part] of this sea, as kings upon thrones, or like kings upon thrones."

The eighteenth point: If someone says: How did He say "Master of the Day of Judgment," when the Day of Judgment has not yet come into existence? How can He describe Himself as owning what He has not yet brought into existence? It is said to him: Know that *maalik* is an active participle from *malaka, yamliku*, and in the language of the Arabs the active participle may be attached to what follows it, with the meaning of the future tense. This is considered by them to be sound, reasonable and correct speech, as in your saying: "This is one who strikes Zayd tomorrow," meaning he will strike Zayd. Likewise: "This is one who performs the pilgrimage to the House of God in the coming year," its interpretation being "he will perform the pilgrimage in the coming year." Do you not see that an action may be attributed to someone who has not yet done it, and only the future is intended? So likewise His words, mighty and majestic: "Master of the Day of Judgment" are interpreted in the future sense: that is, He will possess the Day of Judgment, or in the Day of Judgment when it arrives. A second aspect: the meaning of *maalik* returns to power, that is, He is capable on the Day of Judgment, or over the Day of Judgment and its bringing into being, because the owner of a thing is the one who disposes of it and has power over it, and God, mighty and majestic, is the owner of all things and their disposer according to His will; nothing can be withheld from Him. The first aspect is closer to the Arabic language and more effective in its method. Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaji said this.

A third aspect: it is asked why the Day of Judgment was singled out, when He is the owner of the Day of Judgment and of other things? It is said: Because in this world there were those who disputed kingship, such as Pharaoh, Nimrod and others, but on that Day no one disputes His kingship, and all of them submit to Him, as He said, exalted is He: "To whom belongs the kingdom today? (It belongs) to God, the One, the Subduer" (40:16). All of creation answers: "To God, the One, the Subduer." Therefore He said: "Master of the Day of Judgment," meaning that on that day there is no owner, no judge and no one who repays except Him, glorified is He, there is no god but Him.

The nineteenth point: If God is described as *malik*, that is among the attributes of His essence; if He is described as *maalik*, that is among the attributes of His action.

The twentieth point: *al-yawm* (the day) is an expression for the time from the rising of dawn to the setting of the sun. It is borrowed for the period between the beginning of the Resurrection and the time when the inhabitants of the two abodes settle in them. *Al-yawm* is sometimes used for an hour of the day. God, exalted is He, said: "Today I have perfected your religion for you" (5:3). The plural of *yawm* is *ayyam*, and its origin is *aywam*, which was assimilated. They sometimes express severity by the word *al-yawm*, as one says *yawm ayyam*, just as one says *layla layla'*. The rajiz (a rajaz poet) said: [[This is Abu al-Akhzar al-Hammani, as in Lisan al-Arab under the root *y-w-m*.]]

"An excellent brother in battle on the *al-yawm al-yami*."

*Huwa* (the word *yami*) is inverted from it: he moved the *waw* back and advanced the *mim*, then the *waw* was changed to a *ya'* when it came to be at the end, as they said *adlin* for the plural of *dalw* (bucket).

The twenty-first point: *al-din* means recompense for deeds and reckoning for them. This is what Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Jurayj, Qatada and others said, and it is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ). His words, exalted is He, indicate this: "On that Day God will pay them their due recompense in truth" (24:25), that is, their reckoning. And He said: "This Day every soul will be recompensed for what it earned" (40:17), and "This Day you will be recompensed for what you used to do" (45:28). And He said: "Shall we indeed be those who are to be judged?" (37:53), meaning, those who will be recompensed and called to account. Labid said: "Your harvest on a day is what you sowed, and a young man is judged on a day as he judges."

Another said: "When they pelt us, we pelt them, and we repay them as they give us."

Another said: "Know with certainty that your kingdom is passing away, and know that as you do, so you will be done to." [[In Lisan al-Arab under *d-y-n*: Khuwaylid ibn Nawfal al-Kilabi said to al-Harith ibn Abi Shamir al-Ghassani, who had seized his daughter: "O Harith, be certain that your kingdom is passing away..." etc.]]

The lexicographers relate: *dintuhu bi-fi'lihi dayn* (with a fatha on the *dal*) and *dinan* (with a kasra) — I recompensed him for his action. From this comes *al-Dayyan* as a description of the Lord, exalted is He, meaning the Recompenser. In a hadith: "The wise one is the one who holds himself to account (*dana nafsahu*)," meaning he takes himself to account. It is also said that *din* means judgment. This is reported from Ibn Abbas too, and from it is the saying of Tarafa:

"By your life, the camels of Mabad were not a war against your religion [i.e. your judgment] from Mudar" — [[The *hamula* means the camels that are carried upon. The *judd* (with a damma) is a well of good pasture. The address is to Amr ibn Hind, who raided the camels of Mabad, the brother of Tarafa.]]

The meanings of these three are close. *Al-Din* also means obedience, and from it is the saying of Amr ibn Kulthum:

"And days of ours, bright and long, when we disobeyed the king in them by refusing to submit."

On this basis it is a homonymous word (lafz mushtarak). The twenty-second point: Tha'lab said: *dana al-rajulu* means he obeyed; *dana* also means he disobeyed; *dana* means he became mighty; *dana* means he became humiliated; *dana* means he overpowered. So it is one of the words with opposite meanings (al-adhdad). *Al-Din* is also used for custom and manner, as in the saying:

"Like your custom from Umm al-Huwayrith before her."

And al-Mutaqqib said, describing his she-camel: "She says, when I have spread out her saddle-girth [*wadin*]: 'Is this always his custom and my custom?'" [[*Daraa* and *wadin* of the camel: when one spreads it on the ground and then makes it kneel upon it to tie it. The *wadin* is a girth woven of one part upon another, with which the saddle is fastened to the camel.]]

*Al-Din* also means the conduct of the king. Zuhayr said:

"If you should alight in Jaw among the Banu Asad, in the religion of Amr, and Fadak should come between us..." [[*Jaw* (with a jim), as in the originals and the Diwan. al-Bakri in his lexicon said: "It is a place in the lands of the Banu Asad," and cited this verse of Zuhayr. In al-Qamus and its commentary under *kh-w* with a khaa: "*Yawm Kho* belongs to the Banu Asad." Zuhayr mentioned the verse. Abu Muhammad al-Aswad said: whoever reports it with a jim has erred, and that day was theirs over the Banu Yarbu'. Fadak is a place in Khaybar.]]

He meant: in the place of the obedience of Amr. *Al-Din* also means illness, according to al-Lihyani, and he recited:

"O illness of your heart, from Salma, and it has been made ill."

The Twenty-Third Issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿You alone we worship﴾, shifts from the third person (absence) to the second person (address), which is called tahwin (variation). This is because from the beginning of the surah up to this point, it is information about Allah, Exalted is He, and praise of Him, like His saying: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾ [see vol. 19, p. 145]. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, this was a reward for you﴾. The reverse is His saying: ﴿Until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them﴾ [Yunus: 22] [see vol. 8, p. 324], as will come. "Na'budu" (we worship) means "nuti'u" (we obey). Worship (ibadah) is obedience and submission, and a road is called mu'abbad when it is made smooth (mudhallal) for travelers; this was said by al-Harawi. The utterance of this by the responsible person is an affirmation of lordship (rububiyyah) and a realization of the worship of Allah, Exalted is He, since most people worship other than Him, such as idols and other things. ﴿And You alone we ask for help﴾, that is, we seek aid, support and success. Al-Sulami said in his Haqa'iq: I heard Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Shadhan say: I heard Abu Hafs al-Farghani say: Whoever affirms "You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help" has been cleared of both jabr (determinism) and qadar (predestination).

The Twenty-Fourth Issue: If it is asked: Why was the object placed before the verb? It is said: It was placed first for emphasis, and it is the custom of the Arabs to place what is more important first. It is mentioned that a Bedouin reviled another, and the reviled one turned away from him. The reviler said to him: "Iyyaka a'ni" (it is you I mean). The other replied: "Wa 'anka u'ridu" (and it is from you I turn away), so they both placed the more important first. Also, so that the mention of the servant and the worship does not precede the One worshipped; it is not permissible to say "na'buduka wa nasta'inuka" or "na'budu iyyaka wa nasta'inu iyyaka," so the verb is placed before the pronoun of the object. The wording of the Qur'an is followed only. Al-Ajjaj said:

Iyyaka ad'u fa-taqabbal mulqi...
Wa-ghfir khataya wa-kaththir waraqi

It is also narrated: "wa thammir" (and multiply). As for the saying of the poet (the meaning being: this camel went toward you until it reached you):

Ilayka hatta balaghat iyyaka

This is anomalous and cannot be used as analogy. Al-waraq, with a kasra on the ra', means dirhams, and with a fatha, means wealth. The noun was repeated so that one would not suspect that "iyyaka na'budu wa nasta'inu" refers to someone other than You.

The Twenty-Fifth Issue: The majority of reciters and scholars read "iyyaka" with a shaddah on the ya' in both places. Amr ibn Qa'id read "iyaka" with a kasra on the hamzah and a light ya', because he disliked doubling the ya' for its heaviness and because a kasra precedes it. This is a disfavored reading, for the meaning becomes: "We worship your sun or your light." "Iyah" (with a kasra on the hamzah) is the sun's light, and it may also be pronounced with a fatha. The poet said:

Saqathu iyatu al-shamsi illa lithatihi... Usiffa fa-lam takdim alayhi bi-ithmid

If you drop the ha', you lengthen the vowel. It is said: "al-iyah" for the sun is like "al-halah" for the moon, namely the halo around it. Al-Fadl al-Raqashi read "iyaka" (with a fatha on the hamzah), which is a well-known dialect. Abu al-Sawwar al-Ghanawi read "hiyyaka" in both places, which is also a dialect. He said:

Fa-hiyyaka wa al-amra alladhi in tawassa'at... Mawariduhu dayyaqat alayka masadiruhu

The Twenty-Sixth Issue: "Wa iyyaka nasta'in" (5) is the coordination of one clause with another. Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read "nasta'inu" with a kasra on the nun, which is the dialect of Tamim, Asad, Qays and Rabi'a, to indicate that it derives from "istu'ina," so the nun was given a kasra as the alif of connection is given a kasra. The original of "nasta'inu" is "nasta'winu"; the vowel of the waw was moved to the ayn, so it became a ya'. The verbal noun is "isti'anah," and the original is "isti'wan"; the vowel of the waw was moved to the ayn, so it became an alif, and since two unvoweled consonants cannot meet, the second alif was deleted because it is extra, though it was said the first was deleted because the second carries the meaning, and the ha' was retained as a replacement.

**The twenty-seventh [issue]: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾.** *Ihdina* is a supplication and a plea from the one who is nurtured to the Lord. The meaning is: show us the straight path, guide us to it, and show us the way of Your guidance that leads to Your intimacy and nearness.

Some scholars said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, placed the greatest and the whole of supplication as a subject in this surah. Half of it is a collection of praise, and half of it is a collection of needs. He made this supplication in this surah better than what the supplicant prays with, because these words were spoken by the Lord of the worlds. You are supplicating with words that are His speech, which He spoke. There is a hadith: "Nothing is more honoured by Allah than supplication."

It was also said that the meaning is: guide us by making use of the sunan (ways of practice) in performing Your obligations. It was also said: the root of the word is *al-imalah* (inclining), and from it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, we have turned (*hudna*) to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], meaning: we have inclined. [see vol. 7, p. 296] The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out during his illness walking between two men, *yatahadda*, meaning swaying. From this root comes *al-hadiyyah* (gift), because it is inclined from one king to another. From it also comes *al-hady* (the animal driven to the Sacred Precinct). So the meaning is: incline our hearts toward the truth.

Al-Fudayl ibn Iyad said: "The straight path" is the way of the Hajj. This is specific, and the general meaning is more appropriate.

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said regarding His saying, Mighty and Majestic, "Guide us to the straight path": it is the religion of Allah, which accepts no worship other than it.

Asim al-Ahwal related from Abu al-Aliyah: "The straight path" is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his two companions after him. Asim said: I said to al-Hasan: Abu al-Aliyah says, "The straight path" is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his two companions. He said: He spoke the truth and gave good counsel.

**The twenty-eighth [issue]:** The root of *al-sirat* in the speech of the Arabs is the road. Amir ibn al-Tufayl said:

*We filled their land with horses until we left them more humbled than the path.*

Jarir said:

*The Commander of the Faithful is upon a path, straight when the watering places are crooked.*

Another said:

*He turned aside from the clear course of the path...*

Al-Naqqash related: *al-sirat* means the road in the language of the Romans (Rum). Ibn Atiyyah said: this is very weak.

It has been recited as *al-Sirat* (with *sin*), from *al-istiratat*, meaning swallowing, as if the road swallows whoever travels it. It has also been recited between *zay* and *sad*, and recited with a pure *zay*, while *sin* is the original. Salamah related from al-Farra' who said: *al-Zirat* with pure *zay* is a dialect of 'Udhrah, Kalb, and Bani al-Qayn. He said: these people say *azdaq* for *asdaq* (truthful). They have also said *al-azd* and *al-asd*, and *lasiqa bihi* and *laṣiqa bihi*.

*Al-sirat* is in the accusative as the second object, because the verb from guidance (*hidayah*) takes a second object with a preposition, as Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So guide them to the path of Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 23] [see vol. 15, p. 73], and without a preposition as in this verse.

*Al-mustaqim* is an adjective of *al-sirat*, and it is that in which there is no crookedness or deviation. From it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153] [see vol. 7, p. 137]. Its original form was *mustaqwim*; the vowel was transferred to the *qaf* and the *waw* was converted to *ya'* because the letter before it was kasra.

**The twenty-ninth issue:** "The path of those You have blessed" (*sirat alladhina an'amta 'alayhim*). *Sirat* is a substitute (*badal*, an apposition in which the second noun replaces the first) for the first term, the substitution of a thing for a thing, as in your saying: "Zayd, your father, came to me." Its meaning is: [[That is, His saying, "Guide us," and what follows it.]] "Keep granting us guidance," for a person may be guided to the road and then be cut off from it. It has also been said that this is another path, and its meaning is knowledge of God, Mighty and Majestic, and understanding from Him. This was said by Ja'far ibn Muhammad.

The dialect of the Qur'an uses *alladhina* in the nominative, accusative and genitive cases. The Hudhayl tribe says *al-ladhuna* in the nominative. Some Arabs say *al-ladhu*, [[Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: "Its use with the omission of the nun is permissible." Thus in al-Lisan.]] and some of them say *al-ladhi* [[That is, in the singular or plural, in the nominative, accusative and genitive, as is taken from the language of the Arabs.]], which will come later.

There are ten dialectal forms of *'alayhim*, and most of them have been recited:
- *'alayhim*, with a dammah on the *ha'* and a sukun on the *mim*.
- *'alayhim*, with a kasrah on the *ha'* and a sukun on the *mim*.
- *'alayhimi*, with a kasrah on the *ha'* and the *mim*, and a *ya'* added after the kasrah.
- *'alayhimu*, with a kasrah on the *ha'*, a dammah on the *mim*, and a *waw* added after the dammah.
- *'alayhumu*, with a dammah on both the *ha'* and the *mim*, and a *waw* added after the *mim*.
- *'alayhum*, with a dammah on the *ha'* and the *mim*, without an added *waw*.
