These six forms are transmitted from the leading reciters. There are four further forms reported from the Arabs that are not attributed to the reciters:
- *'alayhumi*, with a dammah on the *ha'*, a kasrah on the *mim*, and a *ya'* added after the *mim*. Al-Hasan [[In some copies of the original: "al-Akhfash al-Basri," who is Abu al-Hasan Sa'id ibn Mas'ada.]] al-Basri related it from the Arabs.
- *'alayhim*, with a dammah on the *ha'* and a kasrah on the *mim*, without an added *ya'*.
- *'alayhim*, with a kasrah on the *ha'* and a dammah on the *mim*, without an added *waw*.
- *'alayhim*, with a kasrah on the *ha'* and the *mim*, and no *ya'* after the *mim*.

All of them are correct. This was stated by Ibn al-Anbari.

**The thirtieth issue:** Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn al-Zubayr, may God be pleased with them both, recited: "The path of those whom You have blessed" (*sirat man an'amta 'alayhim*).

People differed about who "those blessed" are. The majority of the exegetes said that it means the path of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. They derived this from His saying: "And whoever obeys God and the Messenger, those are with those whom God has blessed of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous; and excellent companions are those" (al-Nisa' 4:69). So the verse implies that these are upon a straight path, and this is what is sought in the verse of the Opening, and all that has been said on this point comes back to this. So there is no point in enumerating the opinions. And God is the One sought for help.

**The thirty-first issue:** In this verse there is a refutation of the Qadariyya, the Mu'tazila and the Imamiyya, because they believe that a person's will is sufficient for his actions to proceed from him, whether they are obedience or disobedience, since in their view a person is the creator of his actions. Thus he does not need his Lord for their proceeding from him. God refuted them in this verse, for they asked Him for guidance to the straight path. If the matter were in their hands, and the choice were in their power rather than their Lord's, they would not have asked Him for guidance, nor would they have repeated the request in every prayer. Likewise is their supplication to Him to avert what is disliked, which contradicts guidance, when they said: "The path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred wrath, nor of those who are astray" (al-Fatiha 1:7). Just as they asked Him to guide them, they asked Him not to let them go astray. Likewise they supplicate, saying: "Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us" (Al 'Imran 3:8), and the rest of the verse.

**The thirty-second issue:** "Not of those who have incurred wrath (*al-maghdubi 'alayhim*) nor of those who are astray." People differed about who "those who have incurred wrath" and "those who are astray" are. The majority hold that "those who have incurred wrath" are the Jews, and "those who are astray" are the Christians. This was explained from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of 'Adi ibn Hatim and the account of his conversion, which Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi transmitted in his Musnad and al-Tirmidhi in his Jami'. The exegesis is also supported by His saying concerning the Jews: "They returned with wrath from God" (al-Baqara 2:61; Al 'Imran 3:112). And He said: "God was angry with them" (al-Fath 48:6). And concerning the Christians He said: "They had already gone astray before and led many astray, and they strayed from the right way" (al-Ma'ida 5:77).

It has also been said that "those who have incurred wrath" are the polytheists, and "those who are astray" are the hypocrites. It has been said that "those who have incurred wrath" are those who dropped the obligation of this surah from the prayer, and "those who are astray" are those who are deprived of the blessing of its recitation. This was related by al-Sulami in his Haqa'iq and by al-Mawardi in his Tafsir, but it is nothing [of substance]. Al-Mawardi said: "This view is rejected, because what the reports conflict over, and what the narrations oppose one another about, and in which disagreement is widespread, cannot be given this ruling."

It has also been said that "those who have incurred wrath" are those who follow innovations, and "those who are astray" are those who depart from the sunan of guidance. I say: this is good, but the Prophet's (ﷺ) explanation is more deserving, higher and better.

"Upon them" (*'alayhim*) is in a place of nominative case, because the meaning is "wrath was upon them." Wrath (*al-ghadab*) in the language means severity. A man who is *ghadub* is one of harsh disposition. *Al-ghadub* is a malignant serpent because of its severity. *Al-ghadba* is a shield made of camel hide, with parts folded over one another, and it was named thus because of its toughness. The meaning of wrath in the attribute of God, exalted, is the will to punish. It is then an attribute of essence, and God's will is among the attributes of His essence. Or it is the punishment itself, and from this is the hadith: "Charity extinguishes the wrath of the Lord," and thus it is an attribute of action.

**The thirty-third issue:** "Nor of those who are astray." Straying (*al-dalal*) in the speech of the Arabs is departing from the course of rectitude and the way of truth. From it comes: "The milk strayed in the water," meaning it disappeared. From it also is His saying: "When we have strayed in the earth?" (al-Sajda 32:10), meaning we became absent through death and became dust. A poet said:

"Have you not asked, so the abodes would inform you
about the tribe that vanished, where they traveled?"

*Al-dullulah* is a smooth stone that water rolls about in the valley. Likewise *al-ghadbah* is a rock in the mountain differing in colour from it. A poet said:

"Or a rock in the hill, what protected it..."

**The thirty-fourth issue:** Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "Not of those who have incurred wrath upon them and not of those who are astray" (*ghayri al-maghdubi 'alayhim wa ghayri al-dallin*). It is reported from both of them that the *ra'* [in both words] may be in the accusative or the genitive. The genitive is in apposition to *alladhina* or to the *ha'* and *mim* in *'alayhim*, or it is an adjective of *alladhina*. *Alladhina* is definite, and definites are not described by indefinites, nor indefinites by definites, except that *alladhina* is not intended as a specific group, so it is general. The statement is then like your saying: "I pass by someone like you and honour him." Or because *ghayr* becomes definite by being between two things with nothing in between them, as you say: "The living is other than the dead," "The still is other than the moving," "The standing is other than the sitting." There are two opinions: the first belongs to al-Farisi, and the second to al-Zamakhshari.

The accusative in the *ra'* has two possibilities. It is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) from *alladhina*, or from the *ha'* and *mim* in *'alayhim*, as if you said: "You have blessed them, not as those who have incurred wrath." Or it is an exception (*istithna'*), as if you said: "Except those who have incurred wrath." The accusative is also permissible by taking the verb *a'ni* ("I mean"), and this is reported from al-Khalil.

**The thirty-fifth issue:** The *la'* in His saying "nor of those who are astray" has been disputed. It has been said that it is superfluous (*za'ida*), as stated by al-Tabari. From this is His saying: "What prevented you from prostrating?" (al-A'raf 7:12). It has also been said that it is for emphasis, introduced lest one suppose that *al-dallin* is conjoined to *alladhina*. This was related by Makki and al-Mahdawi. The Kufans said: the *la'* has the meaning of *ghayr* ("other than"), and this is the reading of Umar and Ubayy, which has been mentioned previously.

**The thirty-sixth issue:** The original form of *al-dallin* is *al-dallilin*. The vowel of the first *lam* was dropped, then the *lam* was assimilated into the second *lam*, so two consonants came together: the long vowel of the *alif* and the assimilated *lam*. Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani recited: "Nor of those who are astray" (*wa la al-da'illin*), with a *hamza* that is not lengthened, as if he fled from the meeting of the two consonants, and this is a dialect. Abu Zayd related: I heard 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd reciting: "On that day no one will be asked about his sin, neither man nor jinn" (al-Rahman 55:39), with *jann* for *jinn*. I thought he had made a mistake, until I heard from the Arabs *da'abba* and *sha'abba* [i.e., *dabba* and *shabba*, forms with a hamza inserted]. Abu al-Fath said: On this dialect is the verse of Kuthayyir:

"When the spear-points were reddened with fresh blood..." [[Thus this hemistich appears in all copies of the original and in the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan, but the line as in his Diwan and in al-Lisan under the root (j-n-n) is:
"And you are the son of Layla, the best of your people in witnessing,
when the spears were reddened with fresh blood."
It is from a qasida in which he praises 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Marwan. *Awali al-rimah* are their points, singular *'aliya*. *Al-'abit* is fresh blood. *Ihmarra* and *ihmarra* mean the same: the thing became red.]]

The Sura of al-Hamd is finished, and to God belong praise and grace.
